IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

- claude-seo:seo-drift: SEO drift analysis agent. Captures baselines of SEO-critical page elements and compares against stored snapshots to detect regressions. Reports changes with severity classification. Only spawned when a drift baseline exists for the URL. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write, Glob, Grep)
- claude-seo:seo-ecommerce: E-commerce SEO analyst. Validates product schema, analyzes Google Shopping and Amazon marketplace visibility, identifies pricing gaps, and recommends product page optimizations. Spawned when e-commerce site detected during audits. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write, Glob, Grep)
- claude-seo:seo-flow: FLOW framework prompt analyst. Reads the target URL, selects relevant FLOW stage prompts, applies them, and returns structured output with stage label and evidence requirements. (Tools: Read, WebFetch, Glob, Grep)
- claude-seo:seo-geo: GEO and AI search specialist. Analyzes AI crawler accessibility, llms.txt presence (optional; ignored by Google Search), passage-level citability, brand mention signals, and platform-specific optimization for Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Bing Copilot. (Tools: Read, Bash, WebFetch, Glob, Grep, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-google: Google SEO API analyst. Fetches CWV field data via CrUX, indexation status via GSC, and organic traffic via GA4 for enriched audit data. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write, Glob, Grep)
- claude-seo:seo-image-gen: SEO image analyst. Audits existing OG/social preview images, identifies missing or low-quality images, and creates an image generation plan with prompts for key pages. Does NOT auto-generate images. (Tools: Read, Bash, Glob, Grep)
- claude-seo:seo-local: Local SEO specialist. Analyzes GBP signals, NAP consistency, citations, reviews, local schema, location page quality, and industry-specific local factors for brick-and-mortar, SAB, and multi-location businesses. (Tools: Read, Bash, WebFetch, Glob, Grep, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-maps: Maps intelligence specialist. Geo-grid rank tracking, GBP profile auditing, review intelligence, cross-platform NAP verification, and competitor radius mapping via DataForSEO and free APIs. (Tools: Read, Bash, WebFetch, Glob, Grep, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-performance: Performance analyzer. Measures and evaluates Core Web Vitals and page load performance. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-schema: Schema markup expert. Detects, validates, and generates Schema.org structured data in JSON-LD format. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-sitemap: Sitemap architect. Validates XML sitemaps, generates new ones with industry templates, and enforces quality gates for location pages. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write, Glob)
- claude-seo:seo-sxo: Search Experience Optimization analyst. Performs SERP backwards analysis to detect page-type mismatches, derives user stories from intent signals, and scores pages from multiple persona perspectives. Identifies why well-optimized content fails to rank. (Tools: Read, Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, Glob, Grep, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-technical: Technical SEO specialist. Analyzes crawlability, indexability, security, URL structure, mobile optimization, Core Web Vitals, and JavaScript rendering. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write, Glob, Grep)
- claude-seo:seo-visual: Visual analyzer. Captures screenshots, tests mobile rendering, and analyzes above-the-fold content using Playwright. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.
</system-reminder>

## cfoai
# cfo.ai MCP

You are connected to **cfo.ai** — an AI-native financial planning workspace. This MCP exposes Ari's public product tools for you to call directly. You can both **read** a company's financial model and **change** it: create and edit scenarios, pages, table blocks, Canvas blocks, formulas, variables, dimensions, and data ingestion.

Model-editing tools change the live model immediately and record reversible changes in its
changelog. Connections, access changes, and outbound actions have effects outside model undo. Build from saved data, research, supplied numbers, estimates, hypotheses, or invented
assumptions. Clearly label uncited inputs and their basis in the model and handoff. Create missing
model objects and editable inputs as part of the work. A missing source citation does not block modeling.

## Read the reference before you build

cfo.ai has its own modeling method, described under "How a table shows the model" below: how tables show variables, dimensions, and fields, how a reference reads from the cell it sits in, and how a table's rows and columns are built. `inspect_skills` owns the built-in and workspace skill catalog. Use its `list` block to find a skill and its `instructions` block to read it.

Read `build-model` before creating or changing model logic, variables, dimensions, or saved tables;
`build-visualizations` before adding a Canvas block; and `import-model` before rebuilding a model
from a workbook or export. Each manual contains its complete reference in `SKILL.md`.

Workspace skills hold company-specific playbooks. Read the relevant saved guidance before substantial work.

## Calling convention

- A multi-action tool selects one operation with the block named for that action; single-purpose tools use their fields directly. Supply only fields supported inside the selected block. An `inspect_*` tool reads saved product state; an `edit_*` tool changes it.
- `target` identifies an existing object where the operation needs one, including the destination of a new block. Creation field… [truncated]

## crustdata
People and organisations: 800M+ profiles, 200M+ companies. Employment history with dates, titles and seniority, education, skills, location, headcount over time, funding, technologies, job postings, social posts, work emails and phone numbers. Filter, combine, count and sort across any of it — people who studied at one place and now work at another, everyone hired into a role since a date, faculty at an institution, alumni of a company, who is hiring, who left and where they went, how many match. Live web search and page fetch too.

When you cannot serve a Crustdata ask, or serve it wrong, because of Crustdata itself — missing or wrong data, no filter or field for the ask (even when you worked around it), a server error that keeps failing, a schema or error message that misled you — report it with the `feedback` tool, once per problem, then keep working. Not for plan gates (403), credits (402), rate limits, the user's own mistakes, or asks outside Crustdata.

Crustdata MCP — Code Mode over the Crustdata API. You drive it by writing a plain-JavaScript script (no type annotations — author against the TypeScript-typed tool surface from get_schema) for execute({ code }); the only I/O is `const r = await callTool(name, params)`.

Core rules (they hold for every script):
- **Write runnable JavaScript — NO type syntax.** The script executes as plain JS in a V8 isolate; the TypeScript types are the tool *surface* you read from `get_schema`, not something you write in the body. A type annotation in the code — `: Type`, `as`, `interface`/`type`/`enum`, or generics `<T>` — is a parse error that fails the WHOLE run (zero spend, before any tool call). Author against the types; emit only the JS.
- **One I/O primitive:** `const r = await callTool(name, params)` → `{ ok: true, data, credits_used? } | { ok: false, status, errorType, message }`. `credits_used` is the server's exact charge for that call (data-API tools only; `0` = free/preview, and an async batch SUBMIT — billed at job completion, not on submit) — sum it to track s… [truncated]

## favstash
Use FavStash to save and find creator inspiration, inspect connected social accounts, compare owned content, and plan or publish social posts. Call list_connected_social_accounts before account-dependent tools. If it returns connectionRequired=true, direct the user to connect an account with connectUrl and stop before analytics or scheduling. Use get_social_account_analytics only for aggregate totals/trends and analyze_social_content_performance for individual content or rankings. When a question spans multiple connected accounts or platforms, send every relevant account as a typed query in analyze_social_content_performance.queries; do not stop after the first empty account. Cross-platform metrics are not directly equivalent, and content should be matched across platforms only when its metadata or publish timing supports the match. Follow structured nextActions when a result identifies a useful follow-up. All operations are owner-scoped and plan-limited. Confirm destructive or externally publishing actions unless the user already authorized the exact action.

## openseo
OpenSEO research tools use credits. Proceed with normal focused research, but ask the user for confirmation before planned batches over 2,000 credits. OpenSEO cannot purchase credits or charge cards. Explain unsupported purchase requests without promoting subscriptions, upgrades or credit purchases, or directing users to checkout.

## treg
treg serves external and live data and generative models: SEO and SERP, backlinks, social and trends, people and company enrichment, ads, scraping, image and video generation (Seedance, Gemini Image, GPT Image, Seedream, Veo, Wan) and voice, plus your team's own tools. Flow: catalog_search (say what you want to do, not a vendor name), then catalog_get (parameters, price, measured reliability), then call. When several providers cover one job, catalog_get ranks them by measured success, speed and price; you pick. If a call result invites a review, rate that one call with review(call_id, usefulness, reason?) after using it, then continue.

## zernio

Zernio API server for scheduling social media posts.

Available tools are prefixed by resource:
- accounts_* : Manage connected social media accounts
- profiles_* : Manage profiles (groups of accounts)
- posts_*    : Create, list, update, delete posts
- media_*    : Upload images and videos
- docs_*     : Search Zernio API documentation

MULTI-ACCOUNT WORKFLOW (agencies, multi-client setups):
When a user has more than one account on the same platform, you MUST
disambiguate before posting:

  1. Call accounts_list (or profiles_list then accounts_list with a
     profile_id filter) to discover account IDs.
  2. Pass account_id to posts_create / posts_publish_now, or account_ids
     (parallel to platforms) to posts_cross_post.

If account_id is omitted and the selection is ambiguous, the write tools
return an error containing the candidate list - read it, pick the right
account, and retry with account_id set. Never guess. The legacy behaviour
of silently picking the first matching account has been removed.

1	---
2	type: Identity Profile
3	title: "AI Writing Policy"
4	description: "The central directive for every piece of writing an AI helps produce."
5	created: 2026-08-14
6	updated: 2026-08-14
7	---
8	
9	# AI Writing Policy
10	
11	> **Purpose:** This is the top rule for any writing that another person will read. Every other
12	> writing file sits under it. [Voice](./Voice.md) says how it sounds. [Long-Form Writing
13	> Rules](./Long-Form%20Writing%20Rules.md) says how it is built. `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py`
14	> says what is banned. This file says what the writing is for.
15	>
16	> Adapted from Clay's internal AI writing policy, 2026. The principles are theirs. The wording
17	> and the vault-specific rules are mine.
18	
19	Good writing moves an idea out of one head and into another head, clearly.
20	
21	AI models write fluent text. They do not yet write text you can ship without reading it. As the
22	author, you take the time to confirm that every idea in the piece is an idea you meant to
23	convey. That includes the structure and the emphasis, because the order of the ideas is what
24	decides which ones the reader remembers.
25	
26	Use AI to brainstorm, to draft, and to proofread. Then apply the five principles below.
27	
28	## 1. Stand behind every sentence
29	
30	You own each idea and each sentence in the document before you share it. "The AI wrote that
31	line, ignore it" is not an answer to a reviewer. A reader who finds one sentence you did not
32	mean starts to doubt the other ones. So read the whole thing as if you typed it, because from
33	the reader's side you did.
34	
35	## 2. Writing is thinking
36	
37	The work of deciding what to emphasise is the work of understanding the topic. Skip it and you
38	finish with a document and no new knowledge. Specs, status updates and retrospectives are
39	proof of thought, so the artifact is only half the point. Even when AI helps you think, you
40	understand the problem better after you review the result line by line.
41	
42	## 3. Spend more time writing than the reader spends reading
43	
44	A short prompt that becomes a long document moves the cost onto every reader. They can prompt a
45	model themselves if they want volume. One person paying a one-time cost to cut and sharpen
46	saves every reader a repeated cost. That trade is always worth it.
47	
48	## 4. Longer is not better
49	
50	Length is the easiest thing for a model to add and the hardest thing for a reader to forgive.
51	A long document hides the real content inside sentences that say nothing. When the piece came
52	from a short prompt, ask whether the prompt itself is the better artifact.
53	
54	There is no lossless way to expand natural language. Every rewrite changes the meaning, and the
55	thing doing the rewrite does not hold your actual intent. Readers want your thoughts, even
56	rough. Polish that costs information is a bad trade.
57	
58	## 5. Mark raw AI output as raw
59	
60	You can quote AI text that fails these standards, as long as you label it. "Claude suggested
61	this, do you think it is worth a look?" is honest and useful. Passing it off as your own
62	finished thought is what this policy exists to stop.
63	
64	## How this gets enforced
65	
66	1. Read the piece end to end before you send it. No exceptions for short pieces.
67	2. Run `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` and take CRIT to 0.
68	3. Cut the document until every paragraph earns its place. Cutting beats adding.
69	4. When you cannot defend a sentence, delete it rather than rewrite it.
70	
71	The scorer catches the words. This file catches the reason. A piece can score 0 and still break
72	this policy, because a clean sentence you did not mean to write is still a sentence you did not
73	mean to write.
74	
75	## Related
76	
77	- [Write Simply](./core/write-simply.md) turns principles 2, 3 and 4 into a working method. It
78	  carries the plain-style rules, and the test that a sentence which reads badly usually means the
79	  idea under it is wrong. Always loaded, so it applies to every draft.
80	- [Runtime contract](./core/runtime-contract.md), the load order (the sequence rule files load in) and the checks.
81

1	---
2	type: Identity Profile
3	title: "World"
4	description: "The villain, the vision, the reader and the owned vocabulary. What every piece of writing is for."
5	created: 2026-08-25
6	updated: 2026-08-25
7	---
8	
9	# World
10	
11	Three files decide how the writing sounds. This one decides what it is for. Every article, post, Note and tweet moves one reader one step away from the villain and toward the vision. A piece that does neither has no reason to exist.
12	
13	Derived from 80 published articles, 145 posted LinkedIn posts and 53 tweets. The evidence sits in [Brand World Derivation 2026-08-25](../INBOX/Reports/Brand%20World%20Derivation%202026-08-25.md).
14	
15	## The villain: rented work
16	
17	Rented work is work you do not keep. You pay for it in hours or in dollars, it produces a result once, and it leaves nothing behind that works for you tomorrow. The bill arrives again next month and the asset never does.
18	
19	[Principles](./Principles.md) already stated this rule in 2026-02: rent no platforms. The villain is that rule inverted and applied to the reader's whole week.
20	
21	Three symptoms a reader recognizes in their own calendar:
22	
23	1. A weekly report eats 30 minutes every Friday, and it has eaten 30 minutes every Friday for two years.
24	2. One post reaches 40,000 people, and the next eleven reach 300, because the reach belonged to the platform.
25	3. A process lives in one person's head, so the process stops when that person takes leave.
26	
27	The word `compound` appears 108 times across 17 published articles. Rented work is what happens when nothing compounds.
28	
29	### The main symptom: vibes
30	
31	In 2026 the fastest way to rent your work is to stop thinking. Copy the prompt, accept the first output, ship it, and repeat forever. The tool got stronger and the operator got weaker, so the output belongs to the vendor. The word `vibe` appears 90 times across 19 published articles, always as a criticism.
32	
33	## The vision: the owned system
34	
35	The reader builds the system that does their work. It runs when they are asleep, it improves every time they touch it, and it belongs to them when they change employers. Every hour of work adds to something that was already there.
36	
37	The proof is the two-week test. A stranger opens the repo, reads no chat history, asks no questions, and keeps the whole operation running for two weeks. Pass that test and the system is owned. Fail it and the system was you.
38	
39	## The main character
40	
41	A technical operator between 24 and 35 who already shipped something real. A docs site, a product, a small audience, or a job at a startup that trusted them with scope. They are good at the work and their output still resets every Monday. Nothing they built last quarter does anything for them this quarter.
42	
43	They watch models absorb the exact tasks they built a career on. They cannot tell whether to go deeper or go wider, so they go faster instead.
44	
45	## What is at stake
46	
47	By the end of 2027, most of the tasks in their job description run without them. They either own a system by then, or they compete on speed against a machine. The window is roughly 18 months from 2026-08-25.
48	
49	## The skill tree
50	
51	Each pillar in [Content Pillars](./Content%20Pillars.md) teaches part of the escape. A piece of content earns its place by advancing one node.
52	
53	### Pillar 1, AI and Applied AI
54	
55	- The reader learns to question a default output instead of shipping it.
56	- The reader gives an agent memory, so it stops starting from zero.
57	- The reader encodes judgment into files, so the judgment survives the session.
58	- The reader builds a gate that refuses bad work, rather than a reminder that asks nicely.
59	
60	### Pillar 2, DevRel and Technical Writing
61	
62	- The reader replaces a repeated ritual with a tool they own.
63	- The reader writes documentation a stranger can follow with no follow-up question.
64	- The reader restructures code so an agent can work on it safely.
65	- The reader owns the pipe to every platform they publish on.
66	
67	### Pillar 3, Growth and Content Systems
68	
69	- The reader builds distribution once and reuses it, rather than posting into the void.
70	- The reader refreshes an existing asset before writing a new one.
71	- The reader measures citations and shares, not impressions.
72	- The reader runs a content system that ships without the reader present.
73	
74	## The vocabulary
75	
76	The list holds eight terms. A term earns its place by appearing in the work already, never by being coined in a strategy document. Counts come from article bodies in `SUBSTACK/2_PUBLISHED/`.
77	
78	| Term | What it means | Body hits |
79	|---|---|---|
80	| Rented work | Work you pay for repeatedly and never own | new, the villain |
81	| The owned system | A system that runs when you are away | new, the vision |
82	| The two-week test | A stranger runs your operation for two weeks | new, the proof |
83	| Compound | Every hour of work adds to yesterday's work | 108 |
84	| Vibes | Using a tool without thinking about the output | 90 |
85	| Flywheel | One piece of work that feeds the next piece | 47 |
86	| Digital twin | Identity files an agent reads to act as you | 15 |
87	| AI slop | Machine-shaped prose a scorer can measure | 13 |
88	
89	Three terms are new and five are established. Use the new three until they earn their own counts, then check this table again. Drop `second brain`, because Tiago Forte owns it. `Brutalist efficiency` sits in [Principles](./Principles.md) and appears in zero articles, so either use it or stop listing it.
90	
91	## How to use this file
92	
93	1. Name the villain or the vision in the first 100 words of any long-form piece.
94	2. Name the skill-tree node the piece advances, before you write a line.
95	3. Use a vocabulary term where a generic word would fit, and never invent a ninth term mid-draft.
96	4. State the season and beat from the current season file, or say the piece sits outside the season.
97	
98	A piece that cannot name a node is an idea, not an article. Send it back to `SUBSTACK/0_IDEAS/`.
99	
100	## Related
101	
102	- [Content Pillars](./Content%20Pillars.md) holds what the writing is about.
103	- [Voice](./Voice.md) holds how the writing sounds.
104	- [Audience](./Audience.md) holds the three personas this file collapses into one character.
105	- [Season 01](../SUBSTACK/GROWTH%20STRATEGY/Season%2001%20-%20The%20Owned%20System.md) holds the current 13 weeks.
106

2	type: Identity Profile
3	title: "Pattern Rules"

9	# Pattern Rules
10	
11	> **Purpose:** `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` catches words. This file catches shapes. A draft can
12	> score CRIT 0 and still read like a machine wrote it, because the tell is the sentence structure
13	> and not the vocabulary. Loaded on every writing job, right after the runtime contract.
14	>
15	> Sections 1 to 4 say what to remove. Section 5 says what to leave alone, and it carries the same
16	> weight. Adapted from `core/anti-ai-rules.md` and `core/ai_slop_commandments.md` in
17	> [Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer](https://github.com/Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer). The mechanism notes are
18	> theirs. The wording and the thresholds are mine.
19	
20	Each rule below names the pattern, the mechanism that produces it, and the fix. The mechanism
21	matters. A rule you understand survives a rewrite, and a rule you memorised does not.
22	
23	## 1. Sentence shapes
24	
25	**The copula dodge.** A model replaces `is` with `serves as`, `stands as`, `represents`, `marks`,
26	`boasts`, `features` or `offers`. The mechanism is a repetition penalty. The model avoids reusing
27	the common word `is`, and the substitute implies a relationship that does not exist. Write `is`.
28	Keep `serves as` only where a real function sits beyond plain identity.
29	
30	**Tacked-on analysis.** A participle clause bolted to the end of a sentence to fake depth. The
31	shapes are `highlighting its importance`, `underscoring the shift`, `reflecting a broader trend`
32	and `marking a significant moment`. These clauses carry no new fact. They claim the fact before
33	them matters and supply no evidence. Cut the clause. If the significance is real, write it as its
34	own sentence with its own proof.
35	
36	**Unearned significance.** A claim of impact, legacy or scale with no support in the same
37	paragraph. Watch for `a pivotal moment`, `a key turning point`, `setting the stage for` and
38	`an enduring legacy`. Training data rewards important-sounding prose, so the
39	model asserts importance and expects the evidence to arrive later. State only what the evidence
40	carries. Real significance falls out of the evidence on its own.
41	
42	**The courtroom noun.** A judgment word standing in for a result nobody adjudicated. `verdict` is the
43	current one, and it arrives as `so the honest answer is not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation`
44	or as `the verdict is still out`. The same move hides in `ruling`, `the jury is out`, `case closed`,
45	`indictment` and `exonerates`. Two things break at once. The noun is a metaphor doing the work of a
46	number, and the `not a verdict, it's Y` frame negates a word the reader never proposed, which is the
47	banned antithesis with a straw man inside it. Write the result, the number, or the reason you cannot
48	tell yet. Keep the word where a real decision with named values exists, such as a court, or software
49	that emits one.
50	
51	**Vague authority.** A claim attributed to an unnamed group. `Experts agree`, `studies suggest`,
52	`research shows`, `observers note` and `industry reports indicate` all simulate a source. Name the
53	expert, link the study, or drop the claim. There is no third option.
54	
55	**The false range.** A `from X to Y` span where X and Y do not sit on one spectrum. The sentence
56	`From innovation to cultural change, AI is rewriting everything` reads as coverage and states
57	nothing. Name the two or three real things.
58	
59	**Name-dropping.** A list of outlets, tools or names with no fact attached. `Featured in Forbes,
60	TechCrunch and Wired` names sources and says nothing. The model lists authority to borrow it. Pick
61	one name and say what it said, or cut the list.
62	
63	**Abstract metaphor nouns.** A concrete idea dressed as a technical term. The set is `substrate`,
64	`vector` used for a way, `locus`, `vantage`, `nexus`, `bedrock`, `modality` and `endgame`. Each one
65	reads as precise and hides a plainer word: `base`, `way`, `place`, `last phase`. Pick the plain
66	word. His own working terms are exempt, because he chose them on purpose. `harness`, `flywheel`,
67	`scaffolding`, `surface` and `primitive` stay. The precedence ladder in the runtime contract
68	settles any other case, and it favours his voice.
69	
70	**The aphorism formula.** An ordinary claim dressed as reusable wisdom. The shapes are
71	`X is the currency of Y`, `the architecture of X` and `X becomes a trap`. This sounds
72	profound and loses the fact. Rule 23 in `slop_rules.py` bans the clever one-liner. This is the
73	same failure with a formula behind it, so replace the formula with the concrete claim under it.
74	
75	**The theatrical opener.** A standalone `Honestly?`, `Look,`, `Real talk` or `Here is the thing`
76	placed before an ordinary point. The tell is the fake reveal, because a person being honest just
77	says the thing. The same words mid-sentence in casual prose are ordinary English, so read the
78	position and not the word.
79	
80	**Adverbs propping up weak verbs.** `He ran very quickly` hides `he sprinted`. When the adverb is
81	load-bearing, the verb is wrong. Replace the verb and delete the adverb.
82	
83	**Elegant variation.** The model renames its subject to avoid repeating it, so one person becomes
84	`the researcher`, then `the prominent figure`, then `the key player`. Rule 28 says one word for one
85	thing. This is the mechanism it defends against. Repeat the real name.
86	
87	## 2. Paragraph and section shapes
88	
89	**False balance.** The three-step formula runs positive framing, then a nod at problems, then
90	instant dismissal. `Despite these challenges, the opportunity is enormous` is the shape of
91	analysis with none of the work. Engage the problem and let it stand, or drop the pretence.
92	
93	**Tricolon saturation.** The rule of three is a real device and a model reaches for it by default,
94	because three items look thorough with no need to be thorough. One tricolon per paragraph, never
95	two in a row. Four real items get listed as four. Two real items get written as prose.
96	
97	**The outline wrapper.** Section titles that a template chose rather than the content. The set is
98	`Challenges and future directions`, `Key takeaways`, `Legacy and impact`, `Overview` and
99	`Background`. Each one announces generation before a reader reads a word. Rule 4 in `Voice.md`
100	already demands a heading that states a conclusion, so name what the section delivers.
101	
102	**Fractal recapping.** A summary before a section starts, and another after it ends. Both
103	`In this section we will cover` and `as we have seen` are padding inherited from textbooks. Rule 15
104	bans the trailing summary, and this rule bans the leading one. Write forward.
105	
106	**Diff-anchored writing.** Prose that narrates a change instead of describing the thing. The line
107	`This section replaces the old onboarding flow` only makes sense to a reader who saw the old one. A
108	changelog, a release note and a migration guide are version-scoped by nature and are exempt.
109	Everything else reads coherently to a reader who arrived today.
110	
111	**One-point dilution.** The same claim restated ten times across four thousand words, sold as depth.
112	Say the claim once. Then spend the length on evidence, on the counterargument, and on what follows.
113	
114	**The undone claim.** A later line quietly reverses an earlier one. The hook promises a result and the
115	close hedges it. A post says "about thirty minutes" and its pinned comment says "under one hour". Each
116	line reads fine alone, so the writer is the least likely person to see it. Read line 1 against line 2,
117	line 2 against the body, the ending against the opening, and the pinned comment against the post. Fix
118	the weaker line and leave the stronger one. Never rewrite both.
119	
120	**The echo stack.** Three or more consecutive lines built on one skeleton, such as "The page lacks X.
121	There is no Y. Z does not exist." The model repeats the last structure it wrote, and a person
122	escalates. Make each line add a fact or raise the cost, keep the strongest, and put the rest in one
123	list whose items differ in shape. Swapping synonyms into the same skeleton keeps the echo.
124	
125	## 3. Fill that is not content
126	
127	**Assistant bleed.** The set is `I hope this helps`, `Certainly`, `Would you like me to`,
128	`Feel free to adjust` and `Here is a draft of`. Each one belongs in a chat window, and inside a
129	deliverable each one is contamination. Start with the content.
130	
131	**Cutoff disclaimers.** The set is `As of my last update`, `while specific details are limited`
132	and `based on available information`. Each one is a hedge formatted as content. Say the honest
133	thing once instead, or ask him.
134	
135	**Placeholder leakage.** An unfilled field that ships. `[insert link]`, `INSERT_SOURCE_URL`,
136	`access-date 2026-XX-XX` and `add image if available` all reach the reader when nobody re-read the
137	draft. A bracket from the fabrication rule is deliberate and stays visible on purpose. A bracket
138	from a template is a defect.
139	
140	**Promotional register.** The set is `nestled`, `in the heart of`, `vibrant`, `boasts`, `renowned`
141	and `a diverse array`. All of it comes from tourism copy and press releases. Write the neutral
142	declarative version instead.
143	Rule 8 in `Voice.md` says the same thing from the other side, so say what the thing does.
144	
145	## 4. Formatting tells
146	
147	**Em dash density.** Already CRIT in `slop_rules.py`, so this is the reason behind that ban. Model
148	output uses the em dash far above human rates and puts it where a comma belongs. Do not trade the em
149	dash for parentheses or an en dash. That move swaps one tell for another. End the sentence, or use a
150	comma.
151	
152	**The colon as a connector.** A colon that joins two clauses mid-sentence fakes a cause. The line
153	`The fix is simple: you rewrite the query` adds nothing that a period would not. A colon is correct
154	before a list or an example. Everywhere else, end the sentence. Rule 17 in `slop_rules.py` already
155	bans a colon in a heading, and this is the same tell inside a line.
156	
157	**Bold on every key phrase in running prose.** Emphasis stops meaning anything once it is
158	everywhere. Reserve bold for a term you are defining, or for a label that opens a line. Rule 2 in
159	`Voice.md` sets the boundary per folder. A bold label must earn its place with a new fact after it.
160	`**Performance:** Performance improved 40%` fails, because the label only repeats the line.
161	`**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file` passes, because the detail is new.
162	
163	**Sentence case in an H2.** Every H2 uses AP Title Case, in every channel, and states the claim
164	its section proves. `SCRIPTS/slop/heading_case.py` blocks a miscased H2 and flags a topic label.
165	H1 and H3 and below keep the case their destination uses. A model that capitalises every word of
166	an H3 or a body label is still showing the old tell.
167	
168	**A skipped heading level, or a rule above every heading.** Jumping H2 to H4, or dropping `---`
169	before each section by reflex, are both template tics. Neither is a writing choice.
170	
171	## 5. What to leave alone
172	
173	Sections 1 to 4 are a list of things to remove. Applied without judgement they produce the second
174	failure, which is prose stripped so hard that nobody is home. That output is not human. It is a
175	different machine's output, and it is the source of every complaint that edited writing reads flat,
176	boring and sanded down.
177	
178	**None of the following is evidence of AI on its own.** Do not cut one unless it sits in a cluster
179	with real tells.
180	
181	- Clean grammar and a consistent style. Many writers are edited. Polish proves nothing.
182	- Formal vocabulary. The banned list names specific overused words. It does not ban intelligence.
183	  Leave "ostensibly", "notwithstanding" and "constituent" where they are the right word.
184	- A mix of casual and formal register. That usually marks a technical writer, not a chatbot.
185	- Dry, plain prose. For a runbook it is correct.
186	- One transition word. A single "however" is English. The pile-up is the tell.
187	- One short emphatic sentence. People land points with a clipped sentence. Flag the drumbeat only
188	  when several stack up and inflate the tone.
189	- A salutation or a sign-off. Letters are older than chatbots.
190	- An unsourced claim. Most writing is unsourced. That is a rigor problem and not an AI problem.
191	- A watched word inside a quotation, a title, a proper noun or an example. When the piece discusses
192	  the phrase rather than uses it, leave it exactly as written.
193	
194	## 6. What to protect
195	
196	Removing tells is half the job. The other half is leaving alive whatever was already alive. These
197	are the hardest things for a model to produce and the easiest for an eager edit to erase.
198	
199	- **Odd, specific, hard-to-invent detail.** A real address. A strange quote. "The lawyer who worked
200	  upstairs from my dentist." Models round specifics off and people hoard them. Never generalise one
201	  of these to make a sentence flow.
202	- **Mixed feelings left unresolved.** "I think this is mostly right and it still bothers me." A
203	  model defaults to a clean take. Do not resolve the tension for him.
204	- **Dated references.** Slang, a meme, an in-joke anchored to one year and one subculture. Models
205	  lag by a year, so these are strong human signal.
206	- **A genuine aside or a self-correction.** A parenthesis where the writer interrupts himself.
207	  Machines rarely do that.
208	- **Uneven rhythm.** A nine-word sentence next to a forty-word one. Model output drifts toward one
209	  uniform mid-length cadence. The variance is the signal, so never regularise it.
210	- **An opinion he can defend.** If he can say why he chose a word, that reasoning outranks every
211	  rule in this file.
212	- **A deliberate quirk.** A writer who always opens lowercase, or never uses a semicolon, is doing
213	  something. Match it.
214	
215	**The operating principle is clusters, not instances.** One em dash means nothing. An em dash plus
216	a tricolon plus "vibrant tapestry" plus a "Challenges" heading is a confession.
217	
218	When you cannot tell whether something is his voice or a machine default, the precedence ladder in
219	the runtime contract decides it. Assume it is his, and leave it.
220	
221	**When a draft carries none of the signals in section 6, the problem is not that AI patterns
222	remain.** The problem is that nobody is home. Adding a specific, a stance and some unevenness beats
223	deleting one more banned word. The fabrication rule sets the limit on how a specific gets added.
224	It comes from him, never from invention.
225	
226	## 7. The pass before you hand it over
227	
228	Run this after the scorer reaches CRIT 0, because the scorer cannot see any of it.
229	
230	- [ ] Any "serves as" or "represents a" standing in for "is"?
231	- [ ] Any tacked-on participle claiming significance?
232	- [ ] Any impact claim with no evidence beside it?
233	- [ ] Any unnamed authority carrying a fact?
234	- [ ] Two tricolons in a row, or a tricolon that hides four real items?
235	- [ ] A template heading, a leading recap, or a trailing recap?
236	- [ ] Any assistant bleed, cutoff hedge or leftover placeholder?
237	- [ ] Any colon joining two clauses where a period belongs?
238	- [ ] Any bold label that only repeats the line after it?
239	- [ ] Any metaphor noun where a plain word fits, outside his working terms?
240	- [ ] Any list of names or outlets with no fact attached?
241	- [ ] Any fact, name, number or source that he did not supply?
242	- [ ] Does any later line undo an earlier one? Read the hook against line 2, the body against the pinned comment, and the ending against the opening.
243	- [ ] Cover everything after the opening. Can you still guess how the piece ends? If so, the hook answered itself.
244	- [ ] Did anything from section 5 get cut that should have stayed?
245	- [ ] Did every signal in section 6 survive the edit?
246	- [ ] List every heading in the draft on one line. Does any heading state an outline slot rather than a claim, so it would sit unchanged over a different topic?
247	- [ ] Find the one sentence in the draft that only Atharva could have written: a real date, a named person, a number from his own work, a moment he was wrong. If no such sentence exists, the draft is not done.
248	- [ ] If the piece covers several parallel items, read only the closing line of each one in a row. Do they all sound interchangeable with the nouns swapped?
249	
250	## 7b. Fixing a MED without creating the next one
251	
252	Each advisory the scorer raises has one right fix. The other fix costs four to six rounds of
253	edit-and-rescore, and that is where most of the time on a clean draft goes.
254	
255	**`readability-fragment` and `readability-bullet-fragment`: add a finite verb, never merge.**
256	"Speed multiplier." becomes "A speed multiplier finishes their own tasks faster." Do not fold
257	the fragment into the sentence before it. Measured across `2_PUBLISHED` and `1_DRAFTS` on
258	2026-08-29: adding a verb created a new `ste-long-sentence` hit in 0 of 239 paragraphs, and
259	merging created one in 6. A fragment caps at nine words and a long sentence starts at
260	twenty-one, so a verb cannot cross the gap. A merge can.
261	
262	**`repeated-consecutive-opener`: escalate, do not reword.** Three lines that open on the same word
263	are an echo stack (section 2). Keep the strongest line, make each other line add a fact or raise the
264	cost, or fold the weak ones into one list whose items differ in shape.
265	
266	**`ste-long-sentence`: split at the clause, and check the halves.** Halving a 45-word
267	sentence leaves two 22-word sentences, both still over. Cut to the real clause boundary
268	instead, or drop a subordinate clause outright.
269	
270	**`ste-progressive` and `ste-perfect`: change the tense, do not restructure.** "They were
271	publishing videos" becomes "They published videos". A rewrite around the verb pulls a
272	fragment or a long sentence in behind it.
273	
274	**`readability-long-paragraph`: cut a sentence, do not join two.** Joining two sentences to
275	lower the count is the move that produces a long sentence. The scorer now only raises this
276	when the paragraph still holds a sentence over 20 words, so splitting one is always safe.
277	
278	## 8. Corpus-level shapes
279	
280	Sections 1 to 4 catch a tell inside one sentence or one paragraph. These four hide at the
281	scale of the whole piece, or across many pieces, so a single-file read misses them. The 2026-08-28
282	audit of all 78 published articles found each one repeating across most of the corpus, on
283	unrelated topics, which is what told a reader the pattern was the machine and not the writer.
284	Full findings: [AI Slop Reader Audit, 2026-08-28](../../INBOX/Reports/AI-Slop-Reader-Audit-2026-08-28.md).
285	
286	**The generic macro-skeleton.** Hook, why-it-matters, a numbered list or a run of parallel
287	sections, a recap, a closing call to action. A reader who has read enough AI explainers
288	recognizes this shape before evaluating a single claim in it, because the same headings
289	("Why This Matters", "Key Takeaways", "The Bigger Takeaway", "Wrapping Up", "Who This Is For")
290	would sit unchanged over almost any other topic. A heading must name the specific claim inside
291	its section, not the outline slot it fills. Found in roughly 83% of the audited corpus.
292	
293	**Zero first-person specificity.** Strip the byline and the piece runs unchanged on any other
294	blog covering the same topic, because every example is a generic hypothetical "you" or an
295	unnamed archetype rather than a named person, a real date, a real number from his own work, or
296	a moment he was wrong or surprised. This is the concrete thing a "reads AI" complaint detects,
297	even when the reader cannot name a rule. Every piece needs at least one detail only Atharva
298	could supply, woven into the opening or the close, not bolted on as an afterthought paragraph.
299	Found in roughly 64% of the audited corpus, the single most common reason cited.
300	
301	**Per-item template stamping.** When a piece covers several parallel items (tools, films,
302	terms, chapters, entries in a series), every item runs through the identical clause-by-clause
303	mold: same heading shape, same bolded lead-in, same closing "lesson" sentence. A reader can
304	predict item 4 after reading item 2, which reads as one template with new nouns dropped in
305	rather than several separate acts of thinking. Vary structure across items on purpose: let
306	length, opening move, and closing move differ per entry so no two are interchangeable with the
307	nouns swapped. Concentrated in, but not limited to, multi-part series (Film School in Scenes,
308	Slaying Your 20s, the Uketsu deep dives) and long enumerations (a glossary, a tool roundup).
309	
310	**Announcing significance instead of demonstrating it.** Stock transition phrases that promise
311	weight the next sentence has not earned yet: "Here's the thing", "Here is what matters", "Let
312	me explain", "Here's the part most people miss". Stacking two or three of these in one short
313	piece reads as connective filler standing in for an actual transition. Delete the announcing
314	sentence and let the next sentence open the paragraph directly. If the paragraph reads weaker
315	without the announcement, the claim itself is not strong enough yet, so rewrite the claim
316	rather than propping it up with a preamble.
317	
318	A fifth shape from the same audit is not new prose to avoid, it is a gap in the mechanical
319	scorer: "X is not Y. It is Z." across two full sentences performs the exact negate-then-reveal
320	move that `ANTITHESIS_PATTERNS` in `slop_rules.py` already bans when it is joined by a comma,
321	and slips past untouched because the scorer checks one sentence at a time. Treat it as banned
322	under the same rule until the detector is extended to match across a sentence boundary.
323	
324	## 9. The Wikipedia cross-check, 2026-08-28
325	
326	Atharva ran [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing)
327	plus a companion 38-badge detector list against this file. Most of the 38 were already covered by
328	a rule above under different wording (not-only-but-also, it's-important-to-note, testament,
329	crucial role, the ever-evolving landscape, the challenges-and-outlook formula, the tacked-on
330	participle, promotional boilerplate, chatbot leftovers). The genuine gaps are now mechanically
331	enforced in `slop_rules.py` and `score.py` rather than restated here, see `TIC_PATTERNS`,
332	`HARD_PHRASES`, and the stacked-questions and echoing-sentences checks in `score.py` for the
333	mechanism and the exact strings. Do not copy that list into this file, it would drift.
334	
335	A second pass on the same day built a probe file with one example sentence per badge and ran the
336	scorer over it. That probe found 20 of the 38 still silent, so the first pass had missed more than
337	it claimed. The 20 landed as 9 new regex shapes in `TIC_PATTERNS`, 4 advisory shapes in the new
338	`TIC_PATTERNS_SOFT`, a `repeated-consecutive-opener` run check in `score.py`, and about 50 new
339	fixed strings in `HARD_PHRASES` and `SOFT_PHRASES`. A backtest over 607 files across the vault, the
340	website and the marketing repo fired the new CRIT rules 35 times in total, and every hit read as a
341	real tic. Four dev-blog strings ("sane defaults", "zero config", "zero-config", "batteries
342	included") were demoted to SOFT in that backtest, because Airflow `default_args` advice and a
343	release note for a cache store both used them literally and correctly.
344	
345	Two writer-facing gaps closed with them. `rules_prompt.py` never rendered the tics, so the gate
346	blocked shapes the generated block in `CLAUDE.md` never named, and the banned headings had the same
347	problem. Both now render, and `TIC_DESCRIPTIONS` in `slop_rules.py` carries the plain-English form
348	of every tic. `rules_prompt.py` exits with an error when a tic has no description, so a new regex
349	cannot ship invisible to the writer.
350	
351	One item was deliberately left out. The source list flags a colon opening onto three or more
352	items ("separate ports, processes, and local state") and says so itself: noisy in technical
353	writing, off by default for a documentation corpus. Section 4 already states the opposite case as
354	correct here ("A colon is correct before a list or an example"), and this vault's own prose uses
355	that construction constantly and on purpose. Banning it would fail correct writing, so it stays a
356	human judgement call, not a scorer rule.
