9	# Write Simply
10	
11	> **Purpose:** `core/pattern-rules.md` says what to cut. This file says what to aim for, and how
12	> to tell when a draft got there. Loaded on every writing job, right after the pattern rules.
13	>
14	> Distilled from three Paul Graham essays: [Write Simply](https://paulgraham.com/simply.html),
15	> [Good Writing](https://paulgraham.com/goodwriting.html) and
16	> [Writes and Write-Nots](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html). The observations are his. The rules
17	> and the vault wiring are mine.
18	
19	## 1. Simple is the default, complex is a decision
20	
21	Use ordinary words and short sentences. Keep the technical term and simplify every word around it.
22	
23	A complicated sentence written on purpose is a tool. A complicated sentence written by accident is
24	clumsy. Both look the same on the page, so the writer is the only person who can tell them apart.
25	Never write one by accident.
26	
27	This rule also protects a draft. An edit that flattens a deliberate long sentence has broken
28	something, so read the intent before you cut.
29	
30	## 2. Every sentence spends the reader's energy
31	
32	A reader arrives with a fixed amount of attention. Energy spent on your prose is energy that never
33	reaches your idea.
34	
35	Most readers quit part way through a long piece. Lower friction means more of them finish. That is
36	the entire return on an hour of cutting.
37	
38	Fancy writing moves work onto the reader so the writer looks clever. Do not charge them for that.
39	
40	**What changed in 2026.** The reader now has a model open in the next tab. Ask it your question and
41	it answers in four sentences, with no warm-up and no history of the field. That is the piece your
42	draft competes against, and it costs the reader nothing to switch.
43	
44	So the price of a slow opening moved. It used to cost a little attention. It now costs the whole
45	reader, because the shorter version already exists and sits one keystroke away. The same holds for
46	a padded middle and for a term you left unexplained. A reader who has to guess stops guessing and
47	asks the model instead.
48	
49	Three faults are fatal now, in this order. The piece takes too long to reach its claim. The piece
50	buries the claim under qualifiers and clauses. The piece uses a word the reader does not have.
51	`SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py` checks all three: `slow-lede` for the first, `padded` for the second,
52	`undefined-term` for the third.
53	
54	What survives is the part a model cannot produce: the number you measured, the thing you tried that
55	failed, the decision you made and the reason. Write those first and cut toward them.
56	
57	## 3. A hard topic does not license hard words
58	
59	Many readers do not read English first. Their grasp of the idea often runs ahead of their grasp of
60	the language. Write plainly because the subject is hard. Difficulty never grants permission to stop.
61	
62	The same choice buys durability. A reader ten years from now sits in the same position as a foreign
63	reader today, because the language and the references will have moved.
64	
65	## 4. Plain prose is an honesty test
66	
67	Complicated writing hides missing ideas, and some writers pick it for that reason. Say nothing
68	simply and everyone sees it, including you.
69	
70	So when a sentence resists becoming plain, inspect the idea before you inspect the words. The
71	resistance is usually the idea, and no rewrite fixes an idea that is not there.
72	
73	## 5. A sentence that sounds wrong usually means the idea is wrong
74	
75	Prose that reads well is more likely to be right. The mechanism is simple. You will never rewrite
76	an awkward passage into a version you believe less, so any forced change moves toward what you
77	actually meant.
78	
79	State the claim in the safe direction. Good sound proves internal consistency rather than truth,
80	because a careful liar also sounds good. Read the signal the other way instead. A passage that
81	reads badly almost always carries a broken idea inside it.
82	
83	The diagnostic is one question. When a line reads badly, do not reach for a synonym. Ask what you
84	meant to say there.
85	
86	This holds for writing that develops an idea. It does not hold for a piece that reports finished
87	work, such as a release note or a build report, where the thinking already happened elsewhere.
88	
89	## 6. Two edits that improve a draft with no new thinking
90	
91	**Force a length change.** Take one paragraph and make it a line shorter. The constraint is
92	arbitrary and the result still improves, because a rewrite cannot move away from what you meant.
93	Use it on any paragraph you cannot fix by argument.
94	
95	**Read as the first reader.** The writer reads the draft more times than anybody else will. Read it
96	cold and mark every place where something catches. Then repair the idea at that spot, not the word.
97	
98	## 7. Rhythm follows the idea, never a meter
99	
100	Good rhythm is not regular. A simple idea gets a short sentence. A subtle idea needs a long one to
101	carry its conditions.
102	
103	An even cadence is therefore a defect, and so is a clipped sentence added for punch. Never
104	regularise a draft, and never truncate one.
105	
106	## 8. Writing is thinking, so keep the thinking
107	
108	Leslie Lamport put the stake plainly: "If you're thinking without writing, you only think you're
109	thinking."
110	
111	AI removed most of the pressure to write. The population now splits into writers and non-writers,
112	which is the same line as the split between thinkers and non-thinkers.
113	
114	This is the villain in [World](../World.md) wearing a new coat. Handing a draft to a model whole is
115	renting the thinking. Use a model to draft, to argue and to check. Keep every decision about what
116	the piece claims.
117	
118	## 9. The reader was not in the room
119	
120	Every term has a first appearance. That is the sentence where the reader either
121	keeps reading or starts guessing.
122	
123	Guessing costs more than stopping. A reader who stops looks the word up and
124	comes back right. A reader who guesses reads the next ten paragraphs against
125	the wrong definition and never finds out.
126	
127	Two kinds of word cause this, and only one of them is your problem to fix.
128	
129	**A borrowed term** is real industry vocabulary. `webhook`, `context window`,
130	`fine-tune`. A reader who searches for one gets the correct answer in a click.
131	Leave it bare and the reader takes one detour.
132	
133	**An owned term** is one this vault coined, or bent to a private meaning.
134	`harness`, `load order`, `state file`, `flywheel`, `second brain`,
135	`digital twin`, `ICP`. A reader who searches for one of these gets somebody
136	else's definition and walks away confidently wrong. The internet cannot rescue
137	that. Only your page can.
138	
139	So an owned term carries its meaning where it first appears. Four shapes do the
140	job, and the scorer accepts all four.
141	
142	| Shape | Example |
143	|---|---|
144	| Copula | a harness is everything you build around the model |
145	| Naming clause | a hook, which is a script that runs on its own |
146	| Parenthetical | the load order (the sequence those files arrive in) |
147	| Concepts table | `\| Harness \| Everything around the model \| You own this part \|` |
148	
149	For a piece that leans on four or more owned terms, put the concepts table
150	before the argument. Rule 10 in
151	[Long-Form Writing Rules](../Long-Form%20Writing%20Rules.md) already asks for
152	this on unfamiliar areas, and it costs the reader twenty seconds.
153	
154	Numbers break the same rule from the other side. A paragraph carrying four
155	separate figures hands the reader nothing to hold, so none of them land. Rule 4
156	of the same file asks for a number per claim. Four numbers in one breath is one
157	wall, not four claims.
158	
159	Run the check. `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"`, and CRIT reaches 0.
160	A hook blocks the write while it does not, because this is the rule a tired
161	writer skips first.
162	
163	**Where this came from.** On 2026-09-04 a batch of 49 pieces cleared slop CRIT 0,
164	LinkedIn format CRIT 0 and SEO 0, and a reader outside the meeting still could
165	not follow one of them. Every gate measured the words. None of them asked whether
166	the reader had been handed the words first.
167	
168	## 10. The pass
169	
170	Run this with the section 7 checklist in `core/pattern-rules.md`, after the scorer reaches CRIT 0.
171	
172	- [ ] Read one paragraph aloud. Does any sentence use a word a smart non-native reader would stop on?
173	- [ ] Find the most complicated sentence in the draft. Was it a decision, or an accident?
174	- [ ] Find the sentence that reads worst. Fix the idea under it rather than the wording.
175	- [ ] Take the weakest paragraph and cut it by one line. Keep the shorter version unless it lost a fact.
176	- [ ] Read the sentence lengths across one section. Is the cadence even enough to feel machine set?
177	- [ ] Name the decision in this piece that came from you and not from the model. If none exists, stop.
178	- [ ] List every owned term in the draft. Does each one carry its meaning where it first appears?
179	- [ ] Find the paragraph with the most figures in it. Can a reader hold all of them?
180	- [ ] Read the first 40 words alone. Do they carry a figure, a name, a command, or the reader?
181	- [ ] Ask what a model would answer in four sentences. Does your draft add anything past that?
182	
183	## Related
184	
185	- [Runtime contract](./runtime-contract.md), the load order and the checks
186	- [Pattern rules](./pattern-rules.md), the failure shapes a regex cannot catch
187	- [AI Writing Policy](../AI%20Writing%20Policy.md), the top directive
188	- [World](../World.md), the villain and the skill tree
189	- [Voice](../Voice.md), how the writing sounds
190

1	---
2	type: Identity Profile
3	title: "Net New Value"
4	description: "The bar every post, Note, tweet and article clears before a word is drafted. Non-obvious and tactical, or it does not ship."
5	created: 2026-09-25
6	updated: 2026-09-25
7	---
8	
9	# Net New Value
10	
11	> **Purpose:** This file decides whether an idea is worth drafting at all. The other core files
12	> decide how the draft reads. It loads for every channel: LinkedIn, X, Substack Notes, Substack
13	> articles and anything else Atharva publishes. Adapted from a creator post Atharva saved on
14	> 2026-09-25. The two-by-two grid is theirs. The application to this vault is his.
15	
16	## Only Box 4 Ships, on Every Channel
17	
18	Every insight sits on two axes. Is it obvious to the reader, or new to them? Is it tactical, so
19	the reader can act on it today, or is it only an idea?
20	
21	| | Non-tactical | Tactical |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| **Obvious** | Box 1. The reader ignores it. | Box 2. The reader skims it, because it confirms what they believe. |
24	| **Non-obvious** | Box 3. The reader repeats it to a friend and does nothing. | **Box 4, Net New Value.** The reader saves it and uses it the same day. |
25	
26	Net New Value means box 4: an insight the reader has not heard, with a step they can take now.
27	
28	The source uses a sleep coach to show all four boxes. Box 1 is "get more rest". Box 2 is "sleep 8
29	hours a night". Box 3 is "you build up sleep debt even when you feel fine". Box 4 is the coffee nap.
30	The reader drinks a coffee, naps for 20 minutes, and wakes up as the caffeine takes effect.
31	
32	The same grid in Atharva's own field reads like this.
33	
34	1. Box 1. "Use AI carefully in your writing."
35	2. Box 2. "Put your writing rules in CLAUDE.md."
36	3. Box 3. "Most rules in a CLAUDE.md never reach the draft."
37	4. Box 4. "Put the rule in a PostToolUse hook, a script Claude Code runs after each file write.
38	   Let it run the scorer and return `decision: block`, so a draft with a CRIT cannot save." This is
39	   how `.claude/hooks/writing-gate.py` works.
40	
41	## Run the Test Before the First Line
42	
43	Write the insight as one sentence before you draft. Then answer three questions in writing.
44	
45	1. Which box is it in? Say the box number.
46	2. What does the reader do in the next two minutes because of this piece? Name the exact action.
47	3. Where have they already heard it? If the answer is "every other account in the niche", it is
48	   box 1 or box 2, however well it is phrased.
49	
50	A box 4 insight goes to the channel skill. Anything else gets one upgrade attempt, then it goes back
51	to the idea bank.
52	
53	## Upgrade the Box by Adding the Missing Axis
54	
55	A box below 4 lacks one axis or both. The fix is to add the axis that is missing.
56	
57	1. Box 3 has the surprise and lacks the step. Add the exact command, number, tool name or order of
58	   operations that turns the fact into an action.
59	2. Box 2 has the step and lacks the surprise. Find what Atharva's own build showed that the common
60	   advice gets wrong, and lead with that.
61	3. Box 1 lacks both. Cut it. Polish on a box 1 idea produces a well-written post that nobody saves.
62	
63	A long article can carry box 2 and box 3 material as setup. The headline claim and every section's
64	claim must still be box 4, or the article is a summary of the field.
65	
66	## New Packaging Counts, Invented Facts Do Not
67	
68	The source reports a client who gained 10,000 followers from one post. She learned nothing new for
69	it. She packaged what she already knew in a form her readers had never seen. So box 4 usually comes
70	from Atharva's own builds, numbers and mistakes, which no other account has.
71	
72	The fabrication rule in `core/runtime-contract.md` still holds. Never invent a number, a result or a
73	step to push an idea into box 4. When the tactical detail is missing, ask Atharva for it or mark the
74	gap as `[the real step]`.
75	
76	## Related
77	
78	- [Runtime contract](./runtime-contract.md), the list of rule files that load for a draft, and their order
79	- [Post Uniqueness Check](../../LIBRARY/Resources/Post%20Uniqueness%20Check.md), the five questions
80	  that run after the draft exists
81	- [World](../World.md), what the piece is for

1	---
2	type: Identity Profile
3	title: "Voice, Tone & Style Guide"
4	description: "Specificity & confidence"
5	created: 2026-02-14
6	updated: 2026-04-11
7	---
8	
9	# Voice, Tone & Style Guide
10	
11	> **Purpose:** To ensure all generated content sounds unmistakably like Atharva. See [About](./About.md) for identity and [Principles](./Principles.md) for the underlying philosophy.
12	>
13	> **Above this file:** [AI Writing Policy](./AI%20Writing%20Policy.md) is the central directive. It outranks this guide and every rule in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py`. Read it first.
14	>
15	> **Related:** [[AI Slop Is a Skill Issue -- Bad Inputs Made Bad Outputs Long Before AI|AI Slop Is a Skill Issue]] (the published manifesto on why inputs matter), [Audience](./Audience.md) (who we write for)
16	
17	## Tonal Attributes
18	
19	| Attribute      | Description                             | Example                                                                                   |
20	| :------------- | :-------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
21	| **Direct**     | No preamble. Cut straight to the value. | _"Stop optimizing your logo. Fix your H1 tag."_                                           |
22	| **Technical**  | Use precise engineering terminology.    | _"The latency bottleneck is in the edge worker, not the DB."_                             |
23	| **Analytical** | Skeptical of hype, reliant on numbers.  | _"The graph shows a 20% drop, despite the new UI."_                                       |
24	| **Witty**      | Occasional dry humor.                   | _"It works on my machine, which is the engineer's equivalent of 'thoughts and prayers'."_ |
25	| **Empathetic** | Understanding the pain of the builder.  | _"I know, configuring Webpack is hell. Here's a template."_                               |
26	
27	## The signature
28	
29	Tone attributes tell a model how to sound polite. This section is the part a reader recognises as
30	you, and it exists because 79 published articles opened in five different registers and none of them
31	matched. Added 2026-08-09, see item 17 in `SUBSTACK/TODO.md`. Correct it rather than trusting it,
32	because it was assembled from the vault and not from a conversation with you.
33	
34	**Stance.** Write from a position. The authority is quiet and comes from having done the work, so
35	state the conclusion plainly and let the evidence carry it. Never perform confidence, never posture,
36	never write to sound clever. The register is a well-read adult explaining something they understand
37	completely to another adult, which means no slang, no exclamation, and no straining for edge. You
38	should be able to take any subject, including one outside your field, and hand the reader a better
39	map than they arrived with. Where you are guessing, say so once and move on.
40	
41	**The reference layer.** This is the strongest voice signal you have and the most underused. You
42	think in film, books, games, and startups, so let the analogies come from there instead of from the
43	generic business shelf. A cinematography choice explains a product decision better than a sports
44	metaphor does. Two or three per article is a voice, and one per paragraph is a tic. The reference
45	has to do real explanatory work, because a name dropped for recognition alone is decoration and
46	reads as showing off. Assume the reader has not seen the film, so make the point land either way.
47	
48	**Openers make a claim.** The first sentence states something you believe and are about to defend.
49	It never asks the reader a question, never announces what the article will cover, and never
50	explains who the article is for. If the opener would survive being printed alone on a card, it
51	works.
52	
53	Wrong: "Ever felt like you're living in a dream, even when you're wide awake?"
54	Wrong: "I created this list to help anyone, especially Gen Z professionals and career-switchers."
55	Right: "Most startups do not die because they ran out of money. They die because they ran out of
56	attention."
57	
58	**The test.** Strip the byline and the topic from any two of your articles. A reader who knows your
59	work should still place them with the same author. If they cannot, the piece is written in the
60	voice of its subject rather than in yours.
61	
62	## Writing Style
63	
64	**Voice & grammar**
65	- Use active voice. Right: "Management canceled the meeting." Wrong: "The meeting was canceled."
66	- Address readers directly with "you" and "your."
67	- Be direct and concise. Simple language. No fluff.
68	- Simplify grammar where natural. Example: "yeah we can do that tomorrow."
69	
70	**Rhythm & flow**
71	- Vary sentence structures (short, medium, long) to create rhythm. Example: "Stop. Think about what happened. Consider how we might prevent similar issues in the future."
72	- Mix short punchy sentences with longer explanatory ones.
73	- Use simple punctuation that keeps readers moving forward.
74	- Maintain a natural, conversational tone.
75	
76	**Specificity & confidence**
77	- Use concrete, specific language. Right: "Let's meet to discuss how to improve this project." Wrong: "Let's touch base to move the needle on this mission-critical deliverable."
78	- Choose definitive statements over conditionals. Say "this works" not "this might work."
79	- Avoid marketing language. Right: "Our tool helps you track expenses." Wrong: "Our cutting-edge solution delivers unparalleled results."
80	
81	## Banned words, phrases, punctuation and style
82	
83	Defined in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` only, and nowhere else. Check a file with
84	`python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"`. Add a new ban to that file, never to this one.
85	
86	## Formatting rules, the Atharva style
87	
88	These are persona and formatting calls that a regex cannot make. The banned lists live in
89	`slop_rules.py`.
90	
91	1. Break large blocks of text into bullets or short paragraphs.
92	2. Bold the key insight so a skimmer catches the value. Outside `SUBSTACK/`, mid-sentence bold is fine. Inside `SUBSTACK/`, bold only a label that opens a line.
93	3. Give a code example where one applies.
94	4. Write a header as a conclusive statement. Wrong: "Where they actually break." Right: "The disagreement that matters."
95	5. Link every source and tool that you name.
96	6. Use no hyphen inside a compound word. Write "second brain", never "second-brain".
97	7. Use no hashtags and no emoji, unless I ask for one.
98	8. Say what a thing does. Never call it "powerful" or "best-in-class".
99	
100	## "Before & After" Examples
101	
102	**Before (Generic AI):**
103	"It is really important to optimize your website for SEO because it helps you get more traffic. There are many tools you can use like Semrush."
104	
105	**After (Atharva Digital Twin):**
106	"**SEO is a distribution channel, not a checkbox.** If your LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) is >2.5s, Google penalizes you. Don't guess; use **Semrush** or just check PageSpeed Insights. Fix the speed, then worry about the keywords."
107	
108	## How to edit my text
109	
110	1. Keep my ideas, claims, point of view, tense and structure. Change only what breaks a rule.
111	2. Keep the length close to the original.
112	3. Invent no fact, story, metric or promise.
113	4. Output the edited text only. Add no commentary.
114	5. Stay skeptical. Check a claim before you keep it, because accuracy beats polish.
115	6. Replace "In a world where" with the change and its result, stated directly.
116	7. Replace "Most people do X" with one specific observation or with my own tactic.
117	8. Replace "Stop X. Start Y." with the reason, the condition, or the steps.
118	9. Keep the response dense. Add an example when it earns its space.
119	10. Use an informative tone. State the fact without sugar-coating it.
120

1	---
2	name: banger-tweets
3	description: Create engaging X (Twitter) posts that drive engagement and grow audience. Use this skill when asked to write X/Twitter content, craft viral tweets, or help with X engagement strategy. Triggers include requests for tweets, X posts, or social media content for X. Atharva is on X Premium+, so one post carries up to 25,000 characters and threads are retired.
4	---
5	
6	# Writing X Posts
7	
8	## Gate. Do these five things before you draft a single tweet
9	
10	This applies to every request, including a one-line lazy prompt like "tweets about this". A short prompt does not mean a short procedure.
11	
12	1. **Load the chain.** `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, then
13	   `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`, then `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`, then `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`, then this file. Nothing else
14	   loads for a tweet. Render the load-order (the sequence rule files load in) panel with `python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill banger-tweets --file "<path>" --node "<node>" --topic "<the idea>"`. It looks the chain up itself and runs every scorer that applies, so the checks half is measured rather than typed. `--glob` takes a batch.
15	2. **Check for a matching Substack Note.** Run `python SCRIPTS/socials/parity.py --file "<the tweet
16	   file>"`. It pairs on `series` plus `sequence` first, then `source_blog`, then the title. When it
17	   names a Note, that Note is the material and the source article is not. Copy every number and
18	   claim across, then rewrite in the register below. See the parity rule in `SOCIALS/README.md`.
19	3. **Read `references/examples.md` in full.** It is not optional background. It is the calibration, and a draft written without it comes out as a summary instead of a tweet. If you skipped it, you are about to write the bad version. Part 1 holds real tweets from writers Atharva reads, each with the mechanic named, and it sets the bar. Part 2 holds the same shapes in his voice, and it sets the register. Read Part 1 first.
20	4. **Write the take for each tweet before you write the tweet.** One sentence, stating something Atharva believes and would defend. If you cannot state it, you do not have a tweet, you have a fact. Then name the take's box from `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`. Only box 4 becomes a tweet: non-obvious and usable today.
21	   Then run the opening gate in `LIBRARY/Resources/Post Uniqueness Check.md` on the first line. A tweet whose best fact sits in its last line moves that fact to the top.
22	5. **Never restate a banned word here.** The lists live in `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` and reach you
23	   through `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. The shapes a regex cannot catch live in `core/pattern-rules.md`.
24	
25	Then output this table before any drafts. It is short on purpose and it exists so the work is visible and checkable.
26	
27	| # | Take (what he believes) | Box (net new value) | Shape | Evidence backing it |
28	|---|---|---|---|---|
29	
30	Never skip the table. It is the difference between drafting and reporting.
31	
32	## When a tweet will not start, borrow a winning shape
33	
34	[Swipefile](https://swipefile.com/) holds about 14,000 tagged examples that already worked, including 903 social and X posts, 3,214 copywriting entries and 2,433 advice entries. Each one carries a short teardown of why it worked. Use [swipefile.com/category/social](https://swipefile.com/category/social) for X specifically.
35	
36	Borrow the shape, never the words. The take stays Atharva's and the evidence stays his. A swiped hook with his claim under it is a tweet. A swiped hook with a swiped claim is theft and it reads like someone else.
37	
38	Read the full entry in `LIBRARY/Lists/tools and software directory.md`.
39	
40	## The one rule that fixes 90% of bad tweets
41	
42	**The claim leads. The evidence backs it up.**
43	
44	A tweet that opens by naming a company, a study, a person, or a report has already failed, because the subject of the sentence becomes "someone did research" instead of "here is what is true".
45	
46	Mechanical test, run it on every draft: **read only the first six words.** If those words name a source, rewrite so the first six words say what you believe.
47	
48	```
49	broken:  SparkToro measured their own accounts and found posts with links reach 10x fewer people.
50	fixed:   a post with a link reaches 10x fewer people than the same post without one. meta wrote
51	         that advice into their own help docs. they're not hiding the toll booth. you keep paying it.
52	```
53	
54	Same fact. The first is a press release. The second costs the reader something.
55	
56	When you are handed raw material (an article, a blog, a situation), find the sharpest uncomfortable truth inside it. That single sentence is the tweet. Everything else is packaging.
57	
58	> **Where the angle comes from.** Pick the subject and argument shape from `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Content Formats - 100 Post Ideas.md`, top 10 first. That file never chooses the wording. Everything below governs how the tweet reads, and a tweet that sounds like a LinkedIn post has failed no matter which format it came from.
59	
60	## No links in the post
61	
62	An X post carries no URL. Not to the blog, not to a repository, not to a tool. X cuts the reach of a post that sends the reader off the platform, and Atharva pays that toll on every scheduled post.
63	
64	This binds hardest on anything going out through Zernio, because those post on a schedule with nobody watching the numbers. Write the post so it stands alone and pays the reader on X.
65	
66	Three ways to keep the value without the link.
67	
68	**Name the thing.** "the glossary" and "pocketflow" cost nothing and a reader who wants it can search.
69	
70	**Give the substance away.** The post carries the number, the rule or the step. A reader who wants the rest goes looking without being told to.
71	
72	**End on the claim.** A post that ends on a URL taught the reader that the post was an advertisement. End on the sentence that was worth reading.
73	
74	Never replace a link with "link in bio", "link in the replies", or "DM me for it". Those are the same toll with extra steps.
75	
76	## One post, never a thread
77	
78	Atharva is on X Premium+. One post holds up to 25,000 characters, so the reason threads existed is gone. Three rules follow from that and none of them bends.
79	
80	**Never number a post.** No `1/`, no `2/`, no `🧵`, no "a thread". A point that needed three numbered parts is one post that runs longer.
81	
82	**Never write a pinned comment.** The pinned first comment is a LinkedIn mechanic and it belongs to `write-linkedin-posts` alone. On X the link goes in the post body.
83	
84	**Never split one argument across posts.** If part two only makes sense after part one, they are one post.
85	
86	A file may still hold several posts separated by `---`, and that is a batch of independent posts, never a sequence. Each one stands alone and the reader can meet them in any order. A post regenerated from a Substack Note is the exception: that file holds exactly one post, because the pairing is one to one.
87	
88	Length is a reach decision, not a rule. Short travels further, so stay short by default. Run long when the material is a system dump, or when the post carries its matching Note in full. Count the characters against 25,000 rather than estimating.
89	
90	## Shapes. Pick one per tweet, never blend, rotate across a set
91	
92	A set of 15 tweets that all use the same shape is one tweet written 15 times. Rotate deliberately. You cannot write a greentext about a study, which is the point: the shape forces different thinking.
93	
94	**One-liner / nuke.** One sentence, no context, complete on its own.
95	`your CI pipeline being green doesn't mean the code works`
96	
97	**Deadpan.** States something absurd like everyone already knows it. The flat delivery is the joke.
98	`running the same claude opus prompt 8 times because "maybe this time"`
99	
100	**Staircase.** Lines get shorter, weight falls on the last one. White space does the work.
101	```
102	1,000 google searches
103	415 produce a click
104	360 land on a site google doesn't own
105	
106	that's the open web's entire share
107	```
108	
109	**Reverse pyramid.** Wide, then narrow, then one line that implodes.
110	
111	**Greentext.** `>` lines, sequential, self-deprecating, ends `>mfw`. For things that went wrong. Write the arrow as a literal `>`, never as `>`, because the scorer reads the entity's semicolon as a banned semicolon and fails the file on one CRIT per line.
112	```
113	>read that video outperforms
114	>buy a camera
115	>learn premiere
116	>post to linkedin
117	>reaches 10x fewer people than plain text
118	>mfw
119	```
120	
121	**Fragment.** Trails off. Lets the reader finish it.
122	`prompt caching exists and you're just...`
123	
124	**Cocky take.** No hedging, no "in my experience". States it confidently. Invites the quote-tweet disagreement, which is free distribution.
125	`if your AI output sounds generic you gave it nothing. the model is fine. you are the problem.`
126	
127	**Dry flex.** An achievement stated so flatly the lack of celebration is the flex.
128	
129	**Shower thought.** Sounds offhand, cuts deep, makes people stop.
130	`"direct traffic" is your analytics tool saying "i don't know."`
131	
132	**Story beat.** One real specific moment. No lesson attached to the end.
133	
134	**Heuristic.** Name the trigger, name the correction, give the direction. The reader can run it tomorrow. Strongest shape in the mined corpus, so reach for it more than you think.
135	
136	**Field note.** One mundane place or moment used as a sensor for a large trend. Dated, specific, and it stops before the lesson.
137	
138	**Timestamped contrast.** Two dates, two lines, no commentary. `2008: build an app / 2023: build an app store`
139	
140	**Dialogue.** A short transcript where the contradiction accuses the subject for you. One calm line of commentary after, at most.
141	
142	**System dump.** The long post that lists a real working setup step by step. Every step names a tool and a trigger, every number is real, and it never closes on "comment X and I'll DM you". The shape most likely to run long, since X Premium+ now carries that length in the post itself.
143	
144	Match shape to energy: hurts because true → one-liner or shower thought. Embarrassing → greentext or story beat. Can't believe it works this way → deadpan or fragment. Stating it without apology → cocky take. The visual has to land → staircase or pyramid.
145	
146	## Voice
147	
148	Lowercase reads casual and confident. Fragments are fine when the meaning is clear. No hedging, no "in my experience", no "this is just me". Specificity beats generality every time, so write "4 years" and "$340", never "a long time" and "a lot". Dark humor is fair game and self-deprecation earns trust. Silence the editor that wants to explain the joke.
149	
150	## Hard bans
151	
152	**Hook shapes:** "Unpopular opinion:", "Hot take:", "Nobody talks about this", "I used to think X. I was wrong.", "Steal this", "[Year] taught me [lesson]", "Here's what I learned:", "A thread 🧵". Also never open on a question, per Voice.md.
153	
154	**Thread furniture:** `1/`, `2/`, `🧵`, "thread below", "more in the replies", and any pinned-comment line. All four are retired, see the one-post rule above.
155	
156	**Closers:** "What do you think?", "Drop your thoughts below", "Tag someone who needs this", "Follow me for more", "Retweet if you agree", "Save this".
157	
158	**Constructions:** the banned words, the negative parallelism forms and the tricolon cap are all in `slop_rules.py`, already in context. The copula dodge and the other shapes sit in section 1 of `core/pattern-rules.md`. Do not restate either list here, and do not treat the absence of a restatement as permission.
159	
160	**AI tells specific to X:** perfect symmetry between setup and payoff, every tweet ending on a lesson, a clean three-act structure inside one tweet, explaining the joke in the last line. None of these four is in the scorer, so they are checked by reading.
161	
162	## The judge pass. Score your own drafts before he sees them
163	
164	Run this after the drafts exist and before the six mechanical checks. Score every tweet out of 5 on each axis, print the table, and rewrite anything below 18. Judging your own work feels redundant and it is the step that catches the three failures a read-through never does.
165	
166	| Axis | 5 looks like | 1 looks like |
167	|---|---|---|
168	| Claim | He would defend this in a reply thread | A fact with no position on it |
169	| Specificity | Names, numbers, exact strings | "the best people", "a lot", "recently" |
170	| Register | Sounds like him out loud | Sounds like a caption |
171	| Standalone | Works with every other tweet covered | Needs the set to make sense |
172	| Shape fidelity | Matches the shape's real mechanic | Wears the shape's label only |
173	
174	Three failure modes score low every time, so hunt them by name.
175	
176	**The vague superlative.** "the four sharpest people i read", "one of the best threads", "a huge corpus". You have the names and the numbers in the material you were handed, so put them in. @nabeelqu's heuristic works because it quotes the exact sentence that triggers it. Any superlative without a name attached is an unfinished draft.
177	
178	**Rhythm beating accuracy.** A line that scans better than the truth. Merging two tools into one, rounding a cost up, saying "paid" about something free. Every factual claim traces back to something that actually happened, and the version that scans worse ships.
179	
180	**The borrowed line as payload.** Quoting someone else's sentence and letting it carry the tweet. The reader remembers them, not him. Quote someone only when your own take is the larger half, and never as the closing line.
181	
182	## Before you hand it over
183	
184	Run all nine. A failure on any one means rewrite, not ship.
185	
186	1. **First six words of every tweet.** Any that name a source get rewritten.
187	2. **Shape rotation.** No two consecutive tweets share a shape, and no set leans on one shape.
188	3. **Negative parallelism scan.** Search every draft for the word "not" and for "isn't". Any tweet built as `X. not Y.` or as `this is not X, it is Y` gets rewritten to say Y on its own. This is the single most common construction that survives a first draft, so scan for it by hand rather than trusting a read-through.
189	4. **Character count.** The ceiling is 25,000 characters, not 280, because Atharva is on X Premium+. Count characters, do not estimate. Most posts still stay short, because a short post reads better and travels further.
190	5. **Thread scan.** Search every draft for `1/`, for `🧵`, and for the word "thread". Any hit is a rewrite into one post. Search for "pinned" as well, because that mechanic belongs to LinkedIn.
191	   **Link scan.** Search for `http`. Any hit comes out, including a link to his own blog. Search for "link in" too.
192	6. **Standalone check.** Cover every other post in the file. Does this one still work alone?
193	7. **Scorer.** `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` and CRIT must reach 0. Ignore the flow, paragraph and fragment findings, which are long-form rules that do not apply to short-form.
194	
195	Run `python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"` as well, and take CRIT to 0. It asks whether a reader outside this vault can follow the piece. Every CRIT names a term coined here, so searching the web gives the reader the wrong meaning and only a gloss on the page fixes it. A PostToolUse hook blocks the write while a CRIT stands.
196	8. **Pattern rules.** Section 7 of `core/pattern-rules.md`, run after the scorer. Then section 6 of the same file, because a set of tweets edited flat is worse than a set with one tell left in it.
197	9. **Uniqueness.** `LIBRARY/Resources/Post Uniqueness Check.md`, five questions. A tweet that fails question 1 (his frame, not just the fact) or question 5 (would any other account post this) does not ship.
198	
199	## Output order
200	
201	Show the take table, then the drafts, then the judge table with the rewrites already applied. Hand him the scored set rather than a first pass, because a draft he has to grade himself is work you moved onto his desk.
202	
203	## Where the file goes
204	
205	Check for an existing placeholder before writing anything. One file per topic per channel, never duplicate, never write outside `SOCIALS/Tweets/`.
206	
207	Look for `SOCIALS/Tweets/tweet_[Exact Blog Title].md`. If it exists, write into it. If it does not, create it.
208	
209	```markdown
210	---
211	type: Tweet
212	title: Exact Blog Title
213	source_blog: "[[Exact Blog Title]]"
214	description: "The hook, one line"
215	created: YYYY-MM-DD
216	updated: YYYY-MM-DD
217	posted: false
218	---
219	
220	[the post, immediately, nothing between it and the frontmatter]
221	```
222	
223	A post regenerated from a Substack Note carries `series` and `sequence` copied from that Note, because those two fields are what pair the file to it.
224	
225	Use `source_blog: none` for original content with no source article. Never emit a `#tweet` tag and never emit a `**Source Blog:**` line, both retired 2026-07-27. Never put an extra `---` between the frontmatter and the post, because a stray one reads as a block break.
226	
227	One file usually holds one post. A batch file may hold several independent posts separated by `---` on its own line, and the review desk shows each as its own card. Never number them, because they are not a sequence. A file paired to a Note holds exactly one post.
228	
229	## Output
230	
231	Show the take table, then the tweets. Add one line on why a shape fits only where it is genuinely interesting. Skip emoji headers, skip a "WHY THIS WORKS" section, skip the recap.
232

2	name: write-linkedin-posts
3	description: Write, rewrite and ship LinkedIn posts for Atharva's personal profile as short list posts a stranger can use, in one of six winning templates, then run the checks, the card, the Zernio draft and the in-place Zernio update. Use when asked to write, refine, redo, review, schedule or batch LinkedIn content, fix weak Zernio LinkedIn drafts, or for any LinkedIn post, thought leadership piece or "make this a banger" request.
4	---
5	
6	# LinkedIn Post Writer
7	
8	Every post is a short list that solves one problem for a reader who has never heard of Atharva. Pick one of the six templates in `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Winning Templates 2026.md`, fill it with real facts, and run the checks. Decided 2026-10-09, after Depost's analysis of his last 19 posts.
9	
10	## Pass the Stranger Test Before You Write
11	
12	The reader does not know Atharva, his tools or his projects. Answer these four in writing before the first line.
13	
14	1. **The reader.** Name one job title, such as "a founder shipping a developer tool".
15	2. **The pain.** Write the problem in the reader's words, in one sentence.
16	3. **The takeaway.** Write what the reader does in the next 10 minutes because of this post.
17	4. **The template.** Name it by number and name. Never use the template of the post scheduled just before this one.
18	
19	If the pain only exists inside Atharva's own setup, the post fails. Find the reader's version of the problem, or drop the idea.
20	
21	The insight must be box 4 in `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`: new to the reader, and usable today.
22	
23	## Load These Files First
24	
25	Read `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`, `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`, the templates file, then this file. The banned words and punctuation are already in context from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
26	
27	## Follow the Seven Rules in Every Post
28	
29	1. **Open on the reader.** Line 1 names their problem or promises a list they can use. Never open on I, my, we, our, a product name or a tool name. `li_format.py` blocks this as `self-hook`.
30	2. **Make the list the post.** Use 3 to 9 items. Each item is a short name, then a `↳` line that says what it means for the reader. `li_format.py` blocks a post with fewer than 3 items as `no-list`.
31	3. **Explain every name.** A tool, product or term the reader may not know gets one plain line, or it goes. Jev, AgentZ, Magi, harness, vault and digital twin all need one.
32	4. **Keep only useful numbers.** A number stays when the reader can use it or a source is named. A number that only describes Atharva's own setup goes. Never invent a number.
33	5. **Put Atharva in once at most.** One line of proof is enough, such as "I tested this on 40 of my own posts."
34	6. **Keep it short.** The body runs 120 to 260 words. Each paragraph is 1 to 3 short lines.
35	7. **Close with use.** Write a one-line takeaway, then one specific question the reader can answer from their own work. Never "What do you think?"
36	
37	No hashtags. No emoji in the body, except the 🌱 in the follow line. No jargon a reader must search for. No paragraph a reader must read twice.
38	
39	## End Every Post With the Same Three Blocks
40	
41	**1. The comment CTA,** directly above the follow line. One word in caps, and a real resource. Write the whole line in Unicode Mathematical Bold Sans-Serif, never Markdown `**`. The offsets are U+1D5D4 for A to Z, U+1D5EE for a to z, and U+1D7EC for 0 to 9.
42	
43	𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 "𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗖𝗞" 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜'𝗹𝗹 𝗗𝗠 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗽.
44	
45	**2. The follow CTA,** exactly this line:
46	
47	🌱 If you want to stay sharp on Product, AI, Technology, Marketing and content that helps you grow as a builder, click Follow. I publish consistently and keep it practical.
48	
49	**3. The pinned comment,** after a `---` rule:
50	
51	```
52	---
53	### 📌 PINNED COMMENT
54	
55	{2 to 3 sentences of extra value}
56	
57	→ {one URL}
58	```
59	
60	The pinned comment carries one URL and no hashtag. If no URL exists, stop and ask Atharva for one.
61	
62	Only one ask per post. A second plain `Comment "WORD"` line fails as `double-ask`.
63	
64	## Use the Fixed File Shape
65	
66	New posts go in `SOCIALS/LinkedIn/_WIP/<post-slug>/li_<Title>.md`. Check for an existing file on the topic first, and write into it rather than making a second one.
67	
68	```markdown
69	---
70	type: LinkedIn Post
71	title: Caption Title
72	source_blog: "[[Exact Blog Title]]"
73	description: "The hook, one line"
74	created: YYYY-MM-DD
75	updated: YYYY-MM-DD
76	posted: false
77	---
78	
79	[post starts here]
80	```
81	
82	`source_blog` is the article title as a wikilink, or `none`. `media_asset:` and `media_alt:` are added by `groom.py`. Add no other field.
83	
84	## Run the Checks Until Every CRIT Is Zero
85	
86	```bash
87	python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"
88	python SCRIPTS/clarity/score.py "<file>"
89	python SCRIPTS/socials/li_format.py "<file>"
90	python SCRIPTS/pillars/pillars.py "<file>"
91	```
92	
93	Then read the post once as the stranger. If any line needs Atharva's context to make sense, rewrite it.
94	
95	Render the load-order panel with `python SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py --skill write-linkedin-posts --file "<path>" --node "<node>" --topic "<idea>" --format "T<n> <template name>" --insight "<box 4 insight>"`.
96	
97	## Ship New Posts as Drafts and Fix Old Posts in Place
98	
99	1. **Card.** Make it with the `social-cards` skill in `META/Attachments/li-images/<slug>/`, then run `python META/Attachments/li-images/_kit/groom.py <slug>`.
100	2. **Commit and push the media first.** Zernio keeps an upload for 7 days, and the repo is the copy that lasts.
101	3. **New post.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_draft.py "<file>"` is the dry run. Add `--live` to save the Zernio draft.
102	4. **Changed post that Zernio already holds.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_update.py "<file>"` is the dry run. Add `--live` to replace the text and the first comment in place. It keeps the date, the image and the status, and it refuses a post that is already published. Never delete and recreate a scheduled post.
103	5. **Schedule.** `python SCRIPTS/zernio/li_schedule.py`. Monday to Friday, 5 posts a week at most, 10:00 AM US Eastern.
104	6. **Close the session.** Rebuild the desk with `python SCRIPTS/review/build.py`, then commit and push.
105	
106	`references/pipeline.md` covers the batch review, the patch tool and post day. A batch of 5 or more gets the fresh-agent review in `references/icp-review-brief.md`.
107	
108	## References
109	
110	- `LIBRARY/Resources/LinkedIn Winning Templates 2026.md`: the six templates, the Depost numbers and the three benchmark posts.
111	- `references/examples.md`: rewritten posts that pass every check, one per template.
112	- `references/pipeline.md`: the stages after the draft.
113	- `references/icp-review-brief.md` and `references/patch-brief.md`: the batch review and batch fix briefs.
114	- The retired skill, hook library and example bank sit in `ARCHIVE/write-linkedin-posts retired 2026-10-09/`.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/write-for-one-reader.md -->
# Write for One Reader and One Claim

Name the one reader before you draft, and decide the one claim they carry away. "Load order decides which rule wins" is a claim. "Load order" is a subject.

## Why

A piece for everyone reads as a piece for no one.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/opening-earns-the-second-sentence.md -->
# The Opening Earns the Second Sentence

Write the first sentence so the reader wants the second one.

## Why

The first sentence is the only one every reader sees.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/each-paragraph-answers-the-last.md -->
# Each Paragraph Answers the Last

Make each paragraph answer a question the paragraph before it raised. Cut or move a paragraph that answers nothing.

## Why

A paragraph that answers nothing is a note, and notes break the thread.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/take-a-position-then-its-limit.md -->
# Take a Position, Then State Its Limit

Take a position, then say where it is weak.

## Why

A claim with no limit reads as marketing. The limit is what a practitioner trusts you for.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/rewrite-by-cutting.md -->
# Rewrite by Cutting, Not Smoothing

Rewrite by cutting and reordering, never by smoothing.

## Why

Smoothing removes the edges that made the draft yours and leaves prose that reads correct and says less.

<!-- DIGITAL TWIN/rules/read-it-aloud.md -->
# Read It Aloud

Read the draft aloud. Rebuild a sentence you stumble on, because the idea under it is usually wrong.

## Why

The stumble shows the idea is wrong more often than the wording.

8	# neatHack Rules We Follow

10	Five rules can get the entry disqualified or cost it points. Each one has a control in the repo layout, so nobody has to remember it.

14	## Three Things Wait Until 12:30 PM IST on Oct 10
15	
16	Checked at 9:59 IST on 2026-10-10: `firstrun` had 0 commits and only a `.gitignore`. Entire was off, and the GitHub repo did not exist.

18	1. Never open Claude Code inside `D:\Atharva\firstrun` before kickoff. Entire timestamps every session it records.
19	2. Never run `entire enable` before kickoff.

4	source_blog: none

6	created: 2026-10-11

9	media_alt: "Card titled Report the numbers that got worse: FirstRun v1 against v2 on the same 4 quickstarts, finished 2 to 3, failed steps recovered 0 to 3, cost per run 0.0262 to 0.0200 dollars, time per run 128 to 201 seconds, traced by neatlogs"

11	---
12	
13	You shipped a fix to your AI agent and it feels better. Measure it before you announce it.
14	
15	4 mistakes that make an agent fix look better than it is:
16	
17	1. Testing on new tasks
18	↳ Run the old version and the new version on the same tasks, in the same clean container. Anything else measures the tasks.

10	posted: false
11	---
12	
13	Your AI agent's spend cap is probably a number nobody chose.
14	
15	FirstRun, my agent that tests docs quickstarts, could spend $0.50 a run. The measured mean was $0.0167, so the cap sat at 30x the real cost.
16	
17	Sort every number in your agent pricing into 3 buckets:
18	
19	1. Chosen
20	Limits you set yourself.
21	- Free: 1 quickstart a week
22	- Team: 10 quickstarts a night
23	- Scale: 100 quickstarts a night, with PRs
24	
25	2. Under test
26	Prices you try before you commit.
27	- Team at $49 a month
28	- Scale at $299 a month
29	
30	3. Measured
31	Numbers only real runs can give you.
32	- Mean cost per run: $0.0167, from 64 traces
33	- p95 cost per run: $0.0508
34	- The spend cap, derived from buckets 2 and 3
35	
36	Teams get stuck when bucket 3 holds a guess. At the old cap, one bad month costs a $299 customer 5x their fee.
37	
38	Derive the cap from the price instead.
39	cap per run = price / runs a month x (1 - margin floor) - compute
40	
41	@[neatlogs](urn:li:organization:105668039) traced every run and measured the costs. @[cfo.ai](urn:li:organization:106807285) built the plan and set a cap per tier.

#neatHack  FirstRunAtharva Shah  ·  blog.atharvashah.com
===== """Render one LinkedIn image from an HTML file. python META/Attachments/li-images/_kit/render.py /card.html The page is laid out at 1080x1350 CSS px (4:5, the tallest single image the LinkedIn mobile feed shows uncropped) and captured at device scale 2, so the PNG is 2160x2700. A JPEG at quality 92 goes next to it for upload, because the PNG runs past LinkedIn's 8 MB cap once photos are layered in. """ import sys from pathlib import Path from PIL import Image from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright W, H, SCALE = 1080, 1350, 2 def render(html: Path) -> Path: html = html.resolve() png = html.with_name(html.parent.name + ".png") jpg = html.with_name(html.parent.name + ".jpg") with sync_playwright() as p: b = p.chromium.launch() pg = b.new_page(viewport={"width": W, "height": H}, device_scale_factor=SCALE) pg.goto(html.as_uri(), wait_until="networkidle") pg.evaluate("document.fonts.ready") pg.wait_for_timeout(600) pg.screenshot(path=str(png), clip={"x": 0, "y": 0, "width": W, "height": H}) b.close() Image.open(png).convert("RGB").save(jpg, quality=92, optimize=True, progressive=True) # A 540 px preview, the size a phone feed shows. Check readability on this one. Image.open(png).convert("RGB").resize((540, 675), Image.LANCZOS).save( html.with_name("_preview-540.jpg"), quality=85) return jpg if __name__ == "__main__": for arg in sys.argv[1:]: out = render(Path(arg)) print(out, round(out.stat().st_size / 1e6, 2), "MB") ==== # LinkedIn image brief One image per post, YouTube-thumbnail grade. The bar is the reference card at `META/Attachments/li-images/211-covers/` (read `card.html` and look at `211-covers.jpg`). ## Six Files Come Back From Every Card 1. Work in `META/Attachments/li-images//`. Nothing outside that folder. 2. Build `card.html` that links `../_kit/base.css`. The canvas is 1080x1350 CSS px (4:5). 3. Render with `python META/Attachments/li-images/_kit/render.py META/Attachments/li-images//card.html`. Run it from `D:\Atharva\NOTES` and never `cd` anywhere else, because vault hooks use relative paths. Output: `.png` (2160x2700), `.jpg` (upload file, under 8 MB) and `_preview-540.jpg`. 4. Look at `_preview-540.jpg` with the Read tool after every render. That is the phone feed size. Iterate at least twice. Fix anything you would not ship. 5. Write `META/Attachments/li-images//meta.json`: `{"slug": "...", "post": "", "alt": "", "sources": [""]}` 6. Do not edit the post file. Do not touch any file outside your folders. ## A Stranger Gets It in One Second on a Phone - One focal idea. A stranger gets it in under 1 second on a phone. - Headline max 7 words, and at least 90 px tall at 1080 wide. Big number when the post has one. - Real material over drawn material. Use, in this order of preference: 1. Real screenshots of the real thing: render the live page with Playwright (python) at 2x, or `firecrawl scrape --format screenshot`. GitHub repos, docs, product pages, search results, terminals. 2. Atharva's own assets: `META/Attachments/**`, `SUBSTACK/_COVERS/*.png`, `INBOX/Webinar/`, event photos. 3. Real photos with a free license: Unsplash (`https://images.unsplash.com/photo-...?w=2400`), Pexels, Wikimedia Commons. Record the URL in `sources`. - Photoshop-grade layering with CSS: 3D perspective on screenshots, depth-of-field blur on background layers (`filter: blur()`), color grading (duotone, gradient maps via `mix-blend-mode`), rim light and glow, drop shadows with 2 to 3 stacked layers, the kit's `.grain` and `.vignette` on every card. - High contrast. Text never sits on a busy area without a fade, a panel or a stroke. - Hand-made accents are good when sparse: one marker circle, one arrow, one sticker. - `face-cutout.png` in `_kit` is Atharva with the background removed. Use it at most on one of your three cards, and only when a human reaction helps the story. Fade the bottom edge, because the cutout has a hard crop there. - Keep the kit `.byline` (avatar + "Atharva Shah · blog.atharvashah.com") bottom left on every card. ## Seven Rules That Block a Card

<!--
Before opening a PR, open a ticket describing the issue or feature the
PR will address. An issue is not required for fixing typos in
documentation, or other simple non-code changes.

Replace this comment with a description of the change. Describe how it
addresses the linked ticket.
-->

<!--
Link to relevant issues or previous PRs, one per line. Use "fixes" to
automatically close an issue.

fixes #<issue number>
-->

<!--
Ensure each step in CONTRIBUTING.rst is complete, especially the following:

- Add tests that demonstrate the correct behavior of the change. Tests
  should fail without the change.
- Add or update relevant docs, in the docs folder and in code.
- Add an entry in CHANGES.rst summarizing the change and linking to the issue.
- Add `.. versionchanged::` entries in any relevant code docs.
-->
====
Contributing
============

See the Pallets `detailed contributing documentation <contrib_>`_ for many ways
to contribute, including reporting issues, requesting features, asking or
answering questions, and making PRs.

content.content: LLM and AI Policy Pallets is affected by a large increase in low quality contributions generated with LLM (large language model) or "AI" (artificial intelligence) tools. This adds to maintainer burden and reduces their available time. Our policy on these tools focuses on the human aspect of contribution and growth. Summary ¶ This policy applies to all interactions with our projects and community, not only code and pull requests. We value contributions that are genuinely understood, created, and communicated by humans. If your contribution appears generated by LLM or AI tools, or you attempt to obfuscate that, it will be closed and you are likely to be blocked. Perfection is never required. Your own words and abilities are enough. Do not use LLM tools to translate or "improve" what you say and do. You must carefully consider social, environmental, and quality issues with LLMs before deciding to use them. Explanation ¶ This policy applies to all interactions with our projects and community, not only code and pull requests. This includes code, documentation, tests, PR descriptions, comments, reviews, answers, and all other interactions. We strongly encourage everyone to participate and contribute without using LLM or AI tools. If your contribution looks like it was generated by such tools, or you attempt to obfuscate that, it will be closed and you are likely to be blocked. This policy focuses on trust and quality, but there are numerous other issues with the social, ethical, resource, and environmental impacts of LLM development and use. Deciding to use LLM tools associates you to some degree with all these issues, and is a personal moral decision you must carefully consider first. """Capture fresh 2x screenshots of the local FirstRun site for the social cards. Read only."""
import json, sys
from pathlib import Path
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

OUT = Path(r"C:\Users\ATHARV~1\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--Atharva-firstrun\8af02350-7a0b-4c1e-859f-73dd272ab4c3\scratchpad\social")
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
B = "http://localhost:8841"
info = {}

with sync_playwright() as p:
    br = p.chromium.launch()
    def page(w=1440, h=900):
        return br.new_page(viewport={"width": w, "height": h}, device_scale_factor=2)

    # 1. prism hero, test mode, then hover on Audit docs
    pg = page()
    pg.goto(B + "/", wait_until="networkidle"); pg.wait_for_timeout(4500)
    pg.screenshot(path=str(OUT / "hero.png"))
    btn = pg.locator("text=Audit docs").first
    btn.hover(); pg.wait_for_timeout(3500)
    pg.screenshot(path=str(OUT / "hero-audit.png"))
    pg.close()

    # 2. the knoxctl receipt
    pg = page(1100, 1400)
    pg.goto(B + "/receipts/FR-20261010-091740-help-accuknox-com.html", wait_until="networkidle"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1200)
    pg.screenshot(path=str(OUT / "receipt-knoxctl.png"), full_page=True)
    info["receipt_text"] = pg.inner_text("body")[:3000]
    pg.close()

    # 3. the dbt-core audit receipt
    pg = page(1100, 1400)
    pg.goto(B + "/receipts/FR-audit-20261010-163620-dbt-labs-dbt-core.html", wait_until="networkidle"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1200)
    pg.screenshot(path=str(OUT / "receipt-dbt-audit.png"), full_page=True)
    info["audit_receipt_text"] = pg.inner_text("body")[:2500]
    pg.close()

    # 4. doc-audit boards: team map and top 10
    for key, aid in [("dbt", "audit-20261010-163620-dbt-labs-dbt-core"), ("accuknox", "audit-20261011-054325-accuknox-help"),
                     ("neatlogs", "audit-20261011-050359-neatlogs-neatlogs")]:
        pg = page(1440, 1000)
        pg.goto(B + "/doc-audit/?id=" + aid, wait_until="networkidle"); pg.wait_for_timeout(2500)
        team = pg.locator("#r-team")
        if team.count():
            team.scroll_into_view_if_needed(); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500)
            team.screenshot(path=str(OUT / f"team-{key}.png"))
            info[f"team_{key}"] = team.inner_text()[:2500]
            info[f"team_{key}_rows"] = pg.locator("#r-team .tm-p").count()
        nxt = pg.locator("#r-next")
        if nxt.count():
            nxt.scroll_into_view_if_needed(); pg.wait_for_timeout(1000)
            nxt.screenshot(path=str(OUT / f"next-{key}.png"))
            info[f"next_{key}"] = nxt.inner_text()[:2500]
        rc = pg.locator("a.rcp").first
        info[f"rcp_{key}"] = rc.inner_text() if rc.count() else None
        pg.close()

    # 5. judges page top and homepage tools section
    pg = page(1440, 900)
    pg.goto(B + "/judges/", wait_until="networkidle"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500)
    pg.screenshot(path=str(OUT / "judges-top.png"))
    pg.close()
    pg = page(1440, 1000)
    pg.goto(B + "/", wait_until="networkidle"); pg.wait_for_timeout(2500)
    t = pg.locator("#tools")
    t.scroll_into_view_if_needed(); pg.wait_for_timeout(2000)
    t.screenshot(path=str(OUT / "home-tools.png"))
    info["home_tools"] = t.inner_text()[:3000]
    r = pg.locator("#receipt")
    r.scroll_into_view_if_needed(); pg.wait_for_timeout(2000)
    r.screenshot(path=str(OUT / "home-receipt.png"))
    info["home_receipt"] = r.inner_text()[:2000]
    pg.close()

    # 6. doc-test list rows with View receipt
    pg = page(1440, 1000)
    pg.goto(B + "/doc-test/", wait_until="networkidle"); pg.wait_for_timeout(2500)
    info["doctest_rcp"] = [a.inner_text() for a in pg.locator("a.rcp").all()[:6]]
    pg.close()
    br.close()

(OUT / "info.json").write_text(json.dumps(info, indent=1), encoding="utf-8")
print(json.dumps({k: (v if not isinstance(v, str) else v[:200]) for k, v in info.items()}, indent=1))

usage: post.py [-h]
               {plan,send,sync-media,schedule,respace,list,cancel,publish} ...

Publish and schedule social posts through Zernio.

Reads a tweet markdown file from SOCIALS/Tweets/, publishes the first post now,
and schedules the rest at a fixed number of slots per day.

    python SCRIPTS/zernio/post.py plan "SOCIALS/Tweets/tweet_Foo.md"
    python SCRIPTS/zernio/post.py send "SOCIALS/Tweets/tweet_Foo.md" --live
    python SCRIPTS/zernio/post.py sync-media "SOCIALS/Tweets/tweet_Foo.md" --live
    python SCRIPTS/zernio/post.py list
    python SCRIPTS/zernio/post.py cancel <post_id>

Dry run is the default everywhere. Nothing leaves the machine without --live.
See README.md in this folder for the full SOP.

---
type: reference
---

# Post Uniqueness Check

Five questions for LinkedIn posts, Substack Notes, and tweets. Run this after the slop
scorer reaches CRIT 0 and before you stamp the draft for the review desk. The scorer
checks the words. This checks the point.

Educational content grows a following fast, because people follow accounts that leave
them with something to use. The trap is that facts are public. Anyone can restate how a
thing works. What makes a post worth following is the frame Atharva wraps around the
fact, not the fact itself.

## The five questions

Run the box test in `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md` before these five. A post outside box 4,
non-obvious and tactical, fails before question 1 applies.

1. **Is the frame his, not just the fact?** A post that only restates a public fact
   ("here is how lead scoring works") is common knowledge. A post earns a follow when it
   adds a name, a number from his own work, or a step order nobody else uses.
2. **Can a reader use it in under two minutes, with no re-reading?** Read the draft once,
   at normal speed, with a stopwatch. If a sentence needs a second pass to parse, cut it
   or split it.
3. **Can the reader act on it without messaging him a question?** Every claim needs the
   detail that makes it usable today: the exact step, the exact number, the exact tool
   name. A post that only gestures at a method fails this test.
4. **Does every hard word carry its meaning on the page?** A term a mid-level reader in
   the field would not know needs a plain definition on first use, or it needs to go.
   Jargon that saves the writer a sentence costs the reader the whole point.
5. **Would this post read the same coming from any other account?** If the answer is
   yes, it is boring by definition, because nothing in it is his. Cut it, or add the one
   detail that only he has: a number from his own build, a mistake he made, a name for
   the pattern.

Two more, worth a fast check but not a kill:

- **Sentence rhythm.** A run of same-length sentences reads as flat even when every rule
  above passes. Vary the length on purpose.
- **The opening line.** If it explains instead of stating a fact or a claim, the reader
  scrolls past before question 1 even applies. Run the opening gate below.

A post that fails question 1 or question 5 does not ship. A post that fails 2, 3, or 4
gets rewritten once, then re-checked.

## The Opening Gate Before the Body

The five questions run after the draft. This runs before it, because the hook is the one
line a reader sees for free and the body can only rescue a reader the hook already kept.
Adapted from the hook-writer, post-brief and voice-firewall skills in The $100K Ghostwriter
(Aryan Mahajan's process), cut to what this vault did not already enforce.

1. **Write 5 openings, one per shape.** Use the channel's own shapes: the pattern interrupts
   for LinkedIn, the tweet shapes for X, the hook patterns for a Note. Each carries a number,
   a name or a moment from his material. Never invent one.
2. **Rank them on three questions.** Clarity: does a stranger know the topic in two seconds?
   Curiosity: can they guess the ending from the visible lines? Honesty: can the body pay it
   off with facts he supplied? Ship the one that clears all three, which is rarely the cleverest.
3. **Cover everything after the opening.** If you can still guess how the post ends, the hook
   answered itself. Withhold the answer and show the cost.
4. **Make line two add a fact.** It stays on line one's subject and never reverses it. If deleting
   it changes nothing, it is repetition, so cut it.
5. **Name the one fact the post rests on.** If a stranger replies "prove it", does it hold?
   If it does not, shrink the claim or cut it. The fix is never better wording.

A claim, never a question, opens every channel. `Voice.md` says so, and `li_format.py` flags a
LinkedIn question hook as `question-hook`.

**In a batch,** run the gate only on posts the fresh-agent review scored under 3.0 on `hook_avg`.
Running it on all of them costs more than it returns.

Three skills link to this file: `write-linkedin-posts`, `substack-notes`, and
`banger-tweets`. Edit the questions here. Never copy them into a skill file.

167	## Template 6, Sort It Into Three Buckets
168	
169	Use it when the material is a decision rule. Depost wrote the sample below from Atharva's own topics, and it is the model for this template.

184	(same shape)
185	
186	3. [Bucket C]
187	(same shape)
188	
189	[Where teams get stuck, in one line.]
190	
191	[The better path, in one line.]

194	The Depost sample opens "Your AI agent does not need more intelligence. It needs less access." Its three buckets are allowed by default, requires approval, and denied completely.
195	
196	## Every Template Ends the Same Way
197	
198	The closing blocks do not change. After the question come the comment CTA in Unicode bold, the exact follow CTA, and the pinned comment with a URL. `.claude/skills/write-linkedin-posts/SKILL.md` holds the exact strings.

FirstRun fixed 16 docs pages in fresh containers this weekend. 4 PRs went upstream from 3 of them.

then I checked the other 13 by hand.

10 needed only a container fix: install curl, install the package, make the folder. the gap sat in the bare python:3.11-slim image. the docs were right.

3 were real docs gaps:
Flask: `flask run --host=0.0.0.0` with no `--app`
Hypothesis: the install line skips pytest
HTTPX: setting `r.encoding` after `r.text` raises ValueError

all 3 diffs stay on my disk. Pallets closes contributions that look LLM-made. Hypothesis allows no fully autonomous contributions. HTTPX asks for a discussion first, so that gap went up as a discussion on Saturday.

0 new PRs. read the contributing rules before your agent opens anything. #neatHack

7 docs audits cost me $0.0146 in total. one FirstRun test of one docs page cost $0.0473.

the audit is cheap because the model reads a shortlist. a blobless clone and the history scan run in code for $0. then Jev, a model that returns typed answers, reads at most 200 stale pages at $0.042 per million input tokens. output is free.

dbt-core cost the most: 11,552 commits read, 7 Jev calls, 130,897 input tokens, $0.0055. fastapi/typer cost $0.0001.

the limit: those 7 audits ran before I tracked cost. I re-ran each one on Sunday to measure it, so every audit receipt says "est." a new audit records its real calls and tokens.

run the free filters first, and send the model only what is left. #neatHack

FirstRun's For Judges page maps every claim to the file that proves it. it also lists what I could not prove.

75 of 113 non-merge commits carry an @EntireHQ checkpoint trailer. the other 38 are 4 setup commits from before the first agent session, then site commits. on many of those, the Entire commit hook hung, and I stopped it so the commit could land.

Trail pages and @neatlogs trace pages need a login. so the repo holds the trace IDs and one full exported trace.

one run called 2 Dagster gaps docs bugs. the Dagster docs already covered both, so no PR went out.

---
type: LinkedIn Post
title: Five Lines Every AI Agent Run Receipt Should Carry
source_blog: none
description: "Your customers pay for each AI agent run. Show them what one run cost before they ask."
created: 2026-10-11

---

Your customers pay for each AI agent run. Show them what one run cost before they ask.

5 lines every agent run receipt should carry:

1. Model usage
↳ Tokens in, tokens out and the dollar amount at list price. One of my runs: 10,963 in, 1,941 out, $0.0453.

2. Compute
↳ The containers the run used, on a line of their own. That run added $0.0020.

3. Plan caps
↳ The cost against the per-run cap of each pricing tier. That run used 96.4% of the Team cap and 162.5% of the Scale cap.

4. Proof
↳ A pass or fail from a check the model cannot touch. Mine reruns the fixed steps in a fresh container with model calls blocked.

5. A hash
↳ A hash of the receipt and of every file behind it. One command rehashes them and fails on any edit.

Line 3 changed my pricing. At the Scale price, that run keeps a 52.5% margin, under my 70% floor.

I built these receipts into FirstRun, my agent that tests docs quickstarts, at the #neatHack hackathon. @[cfo.ai](urn:li:organization:106807285) set the caps from measured costs.

Print the receipt before you set the price.

Which of the 5 lines would your last agent run fail?

---
type: LinkedIn Post
title: Find the Docs Areas That Rest on One Person
source_blog: none
description: "Your docs may depend on one person, and nobody wrote that down."
created: 2026-10-11
updated: 2026-10-11
posted: false
---

Your docs may depend on one person, and nobody wrote that down.

When that person takes leave, every page they own stops changing.

Here is the check in 4 steps:

1. Count files changed per person, and ignore line counts
↳ Cap each commit's weight, so a 250-file rename weighs the same as 4 small commits.

2. Halve a commit's weight every 90 days
↳ Recent work shows who knows an area today.

3. Drop the bots and keep emails off the page
↳ Show names and public logins only, and let anyone opt out.

4. Rank the next 10 docs tasks and suggest an owner for each
↳ Cite the commits and the dates behind each task, so anyone can check the pick.

I ran this check on the AccuKnox help docs I maintain, with FirstRun, the docs agent I built at the #neatHack hackathon. 9 of 9 areas rest on one person, and that person is me. 8 of the top 10 tasks name me.

The same check on dbt-core names 12 people, groups 231 more, and finds no area that rests on one person.

If one name owns every area, write the handover doc first.

Which docs area would stop changing if you left for a month?

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 "𝗠𝗔𝗣" 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜'𝗹𝗹 𝗗𝗠 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝗽.
🌱 If you want to stay sharp on Product, AI, Technology, Marketing and content that helps you grow as a builder, click Follow. I publish consistently and keep it practical.

---
### 📌 PINNED COMMENT

The map reads 12 months of public commits from the repo. On the AccuKnox board, each task says Jev, the model that reads the pages, did not read it, so treat that ranking as a first pass.

→ https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/doc-audit/?id=audit-20261011-054325-accuknox-help

content.content:
"""Wire each finished card into its LinkedIn post and add the standard pinned-comment links.

    python META/Attachments/li-images/_kit/groom.py            # every slug with a meta.json
    python META/Attachments/li-images/_kit/groom.py <slug> ...

For each meta.json it:
  1. sets `media_asset:` to the card JPG and `media_alt:` to the alt text,
  2. marks `media_status: done` when that field exists,
  3. gives the pinned comment one link (the blog when it has none), and a book-a-call line only
     when meta.json carries "offer": true (a rung 2 post, see Audience-First Offer System),
  4. drops leftover placeholder warnings from the pinned comment.
"""
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[4]
CARDS = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
BLOG = "→ More from me every week: https://blog.atharvashah.com"
BOOK = "→ Want this set up for your team? Book a call: https://atharvashah.com/#bookmeeting"


def set_field(fm: str, key: str, value: str) -> str:
    line = f'{key}: "{value}"'
    if re.search(rf"^{key}:.*$", fm, re.M):
        return re.sub(rf"^{key}:.*$", lambda _: line, fm, count=1, flags=re.M)
    return re.sub(r"^posted:", lambda _: f"{line}\nposted:", fm, count=1, flags=re.M)


def groom(meta: Path) -> str:
    d = json.loads(meta.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    post = ROOT / d["post"]
    raw = post.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    m = re.match(r"^---\n(.*?)\n---\n", raw, re.S)
    fm, body = m.group(1), raw[m.end():]
    depth = len(Path(d["post"]).parts) - 1
    rel = "../" * depth + f"META/Attachments/li-images/{d['slug']}/{d['slug']}.jpg"
    fm = set_field(fm, "media_asset", rel)
    fm = set_field(fm, "media_alt", d["alt"].replace('"', "'"))

## The Launch Features Add Six Beats About Cost, Ownership and Restraint

PR #54 merged on 2026-10-11 and put five features on the live site. They go into the same Wednesday article as a second half, after "What it cost". Every number below was checked against the `firstrun` repo on 2026-10-11 at about 17:00 IST.

**Section title:** "The Agent Printed a Receipt, Then Refused to Open 12 PRs"

**Thesis:** "A docs agent earns trust when it shows the bill for each run and declines the work a repo's rules forbid." This is box 4, because a reader can add a receipt and a contributing-rules check to their own agent today.

**World node:** builds a gate that refuses bad work, rather than a reminder that asks nicely.

| # | Beat, the claim it proves | Exact numbers | Source in `firstrun` | Screenshot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The hero shows only real failures | Errors such as `No such option: --years` and `entire: command not found`. 6 results leave the prism. Hover on Audit docs shows a flags page 453 days old and 72 features with no docs | `docs/assets/prism.js` line 16 comment and the `POOL` list, `docs/index.html` | `META/Attachments/neathack/x/x2-prism-hero.jpg` |
| 2 | Every run ends with a bill | AccuKnox knoxctl: model $0.0453 (10,963 in, 1,941 out), compute $0.0020, total $0.0473. Team cap $0.04697 at 96.4%, Scale cap $0.02787 at 162.5%, Free at 334.3%. Scale margin 52.5%, under the 70% floor. 5 of 5 steps verified. 76 receipts in `docs/receipts/` | `docs/receipts/FR-20261010-091740-help-accuknox-com.json`, `src/firstrun/receipt.py`. `firstrun receipt --check` printed "ok" on 2026-10-11 | `x/x3-receipt-knoxctl.jpg`, `li-images/firstrun-neathack-receipts/` |
| 3 | An audit costs less than one run | 7 audits cost $0.014609 in total, from $0.000101 (fastapi/typer) to $0.005498 (dbt-core: 7 Jev calls, 130,897 input tokens, 11,552 commits). Jev input at $0.042 per million tokens. All 7 are estimates from a re-run on 2026-10-11 | `cost` field in `docs/audits/audit-*.json` | `x/x4-audit-costs.jpg` |
| 4 | The team map finds the single owner | AccuKnox/help: 9 of 9 areas rest on one person, and that person is Atharva (425 commits). 8 of its top 10 tasks name him, 2 have no clear owner. dbt-core: 247 people, the map names 12 and groups 231, no area on one person. neatlogs: 1 of 6 areas, `scripts/compatibility/` | `team` and `next` fields in `docs/audits/*.json`, `src/firstrun/team.py`, README "Team map and privacy" | `x/x5-team-map.jpg`, `li-images/firstrun-neathack-team-map/` |
| 5 | The proof page lists its own gaps | 75 of 113 non-merge commits carry an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer, 38 do not. Trail and neatlogs trace pages need a login. 360 offline tests pass on main (CI run 38135341435) | `docs/judges/index.html`, `evidence/entire.md` | `x/x7-judges-proof-map.jpg` |
| 6 | The agent declined 12 PRs | 16 pages fixed and verified. 3 pages became 4 PRs. Of the other 13, 10 needed only a container fix and 3 had real gaps: Flask (`flask run` with no `--app`), Hypothesis (install line skips pytest), HTTPX (`r.encoding` after `r.text`). The Pallets LLM policy, the Hypothesis AI policy and the HTTPX discussion-first rule held all 3. 0 new PRs. The HTTPX gap went up as discussion #3801 on Saturday | `docs/runs/index.json`, `docs/data/prs.json`, the three diffs in the session scratchpad `proposed/` folder | `x/x6-zero-new-prs.jpg` |

Beat 6 carries the article's honest close. Two facts sit beside it: the HTTPX discussion #3801 and the Polars issue #29855 both went up by hand on Saturday, so the record says "0 new PRs", never "nothing filed".

The six X posts that pair with these beats are in [38 Post Ship List Sun](38%20Post%20Ship%20List%20Sun.md), rows X2 to X7. Embed each one by its live URL once it goes out.

> the audit is cheap because the model reads a shortlist. a blobless clone and the history scan run in code for $0. then Jev, a model that returns typed answers, reads at most 200 stale pages at $0.042 per million input tokens. output is free.
